issues.body:
## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| OpenClaw | `2026.10.6 (fe06181)`, updated from 2026.9.x on 2026-10-23. All observations before 23.10 come from 2026.9.x. |
| Node | `v26.12.1` |
| OS | Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, kernel 7.0.0, Hetzner vServer, 16 vCPU, 30 GiB RAM, **no swap** |
| Service | systemd system unit `openclaw-gateway.service`, `MemoryHigh=12G`, `MemoryMax=16G`, `Restart=always` |
| Plugins | 21 loaded at the latest start: anthropic, browser, canvas, codex, cua-computer, device-pair, file-transfer, geolocation, github, linux-node, memory-core, ollama, openai, outbound-markup-guard, perplexity, talk-voice, telegram, xai, plus 3 local workspace plugins. Before 2026-10-26 the count was 18 (19 or 20 during today's rollout). |
| Channels | 2 Telegram bot accounts (forum topics), cron jobs (315 defined), CLI-backed agents (`claude`, `codex`) and the `browser` tool (Chrome) as child processes |
| Same host | Ollama (`llama-server`), Docker (Postgres), and a few Python services |

## 1. Memory growth and OOM kill

### Observed

- On **2026-10-15 22:15:53** a global (not cgroup-constrained) OOM killed the gateway unit after **4 d 4 h 12 min** of uptime:

  ```
  kernel: llama-server invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x140dca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE|__GFP_ZERO|__GFP_COMP), order=0, oom_score_adj=0
  kernel: oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_NONE,nodemask=(null),cpuset=ollama.service,mems_allowed=0,global_oom,task_memcg=/system.slice/openclaw-gateway.service,task=python,pid=<pid>,uid=1000
  systemd[1]: openclaw-gateway.service: The kernel OOM killer killed some processes in this unit.
  systemd[1]: openclaw-gateway.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
  systemd[1]: openclaw-gateway.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.
  systemd[1]: openclaw-gateway.service: Consumed 3d 22h 54min 20.986s CPU time over 4d 4h 12min 18.585s wall clock time, 22.9G memory peak.
  ```

- **Breakdown at OOM time.** I summed the kernel task table by process name (RSS only):

  | process | count | RSS |
  |---|---|---|
  | chrome (browser tool) | 21 | 4.04 GiB |
  | openclaw-gateway (main) | 1 | **3.40 GiB** |
  | node-MainThread (workers / MCP children) | 51 | 2.06 GiB |
  | claude (CLI agent) | 9 + 5 | 2.51 GiB |
  | MainThread | 22 | 1.72 GiB |
  | llama-server (Ollama, other unit) | 1 | 1.29 GiB |
  | npm (`npm exec` MCP servers) | 13 | 0.61 GiB |
  | codex | 5 | 0.38 GiB |
  | all tasks | | 18.97 GiB |

  The kernel also reported `shmem:2522146` pages, about **9.6 GiB** of shared memory. The 22.9 GB cgroup peak is therefore mostly **child processes plus shmem** charged to the gateway unit, not the gateway's own heap.

- **The gateway main process grows on every run.** These values come from the gateway's own `[diagnostics/memory]` lines. Each row is one process lifetime between restarts:

  | first sample | RSS / heapUsed | last sample | RSS / heapUsed | max RSS |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 10-14 07:06 (process up since 10-11 18:03) | 3.11 / 0.79 GiB | 10-15 22:13 (OOM 2 min later) | 3.18 / 0.92 GiB | 3.55 GiB |
  | 10-15 22:30 | 2.13 / 0.65 | 10-17 20:37 | 2.71 / 0.63 | 2.72 |
  | 10-18 01:07 | 1.82 / 0.37 | 10-18 18:05 | 2.23 / 0.62 | 2.80 |
  | 10-18 18:23 | 1.80 / 0.39 | 10-20 09:35 | 2.79 / 0.74 | 3.13 |
  | 10-20 09:45 | 2.09 / 0.77 | 10-22 21:31 | 2.90 / 0.72 | 3.09 |
  | 10-22 21:51 | 1.74 / 0.35 | 10-23 18:01 | 2.44 / 0.56 | 2.72 |

  Pattern: RSS starts around 1.8 GiB and reaches 2.7 to 3.5 GiB after 1 to 4 days. heapUsed roughly doubles (0.35 to 0.75 GiB). The unit's cgroup peak per run was 18 to 22 GB on every multi-day run, for example `22.4G memory peak` after 2 d 11 h and `20G memory peak` after 1 d 15 h.

- **Memory-pressure diagnostics.** The journal holds 2,789 lines of `[diagnostics/memory] memory pressure` (2,421 `level=warning` at the 2.05 GiB threshold, 368 `level=critical` at 3.07 GiB). They appear on every day from 10-14 to 10-23. Since the 2026.10.6 update (10-23 18:36) none have appeared, but the gateway has also not run longer than about 44 h since then. Sample line (worker numbers cut off):

  ```
  [diagnostics/memory] memory pressure: level=critical reason=rss_threshold rss=3.21 GiB heap=935.9 MiB threshold=3.07 GiB thresholdRatio=104.5% rssBytes=3445874688 heapUsedBytes=981350616 externalBytes=133240436 arrayBuffersBytes=120809201 workerHeapTotalBytes=513036288 workerHeapUsedBytes=431401304 …
  ```

- **`MaxListenersExceededWarning`, 26 times.** It fired once in each of 26 distinct gateway PIDs, which matches the 26 starts in the journal. It appears 1 to 2 s after `http server listening`. It is always the same listener and count:

  ```
  (node:<pid>) MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 exit listeners added to [process]. MaxListeners is 10. Use emitter.setMaxListeners() to increase limit
  ```

  Per day: 10-15: 1, 10-17: 1, 10-18: 2, 10-20: 1, 10-22: 1, 10-23: 3, 10-25: 3, 10-26: 14 (many restarts that day). So the count is set at startup, probably one `process.on('exit')` per plugin or child supervisor. It does not grow during runtime. It is reported here because it suggests that exit handlers or child supervisors are registered without being removed, which fits the leftover child processes in the OOM table.

### Expected

- The gateway's RSS stays flat once the process has warmed up.
- Child processes the gateway spawns are reaped when the turn, session or tool that owns them ends. In the OOM table that means `browser` Chrome instances, `claude` and `codex` CLI agents, and `npm exec` MCP servers.
- The unit does not reach a 20 GB cgroup peak on a 30 GiB host.

### Actual

- RSS grows by about 1 GiB over 2 to 4 days.
- Child processes pile up: 21 chrome, 14 claude, 51 node worker threads and 13 `npm exec` at OOM time.
- About 9.6 GiB of shmem is charged.
- With no swap, a global OOM kills the whole unit, and the turns in flight are lost.

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is there a supported way to cap the browser tool's Chrome instances and the CLI-agent children per gateway (pool size, idle reaping)?
2. Is the shmem charge expected from Chrome (`/dev/shm`) under the gateway cgroup? Would `--disable-dev-shm-usage` be a reasonable default for headless use?
3. Which subsystem registers the 11 `process` `exit` listeners at startup? Running `node --trace-warnings` could pinpoint it if you tell us how to pass Node flags to the gateway entry.

## 2. Slow startup: 56 to 125 s from `Started` to `http server listening`

### Observed

I measured 26 starts as the time between systemd `Started openclaw-gateway.service` and `[gateway] http server listening`: **min 56 s, median 81 s, max 125 s**. The worst start (125 s) was the restart right after the OOM on 10-15. On 2026.10.6 the range is 56 to 102 s (20 starts). The gateway's own figure in the listening line is lower, for example `http server listening (21 plugins: …; 46.2s)` against 70 s measured by systemd.

Phase timings for the start on 2026-10-26 16:34:54 (2026.10.6, 21 plugins). Only phases of 1 s or more are listed; `t` is the gateway's running total:

```
cli.main.gateway-run-select-environment        5591 ms  (t=6.7s)
cli.main.gateway-run-pre-bootstrap             2713 ms  (t=9.6s)
cli.bootstrap.admission.database-readiness     3693 ms  (t=14.6s)   agentCount=3
cli.bootstrap.admission.state-snapshot         6685 ms  (t=16.4s)
cli.bootstrap.gateway-lock                     4004 ms  (t=23.6s)
cli.bootstrap.boot-lifecycle                   2574 ms  (t=26.3s)
process.bootstrap                             28188 ms  (t=28.2s)
config.auth                                   17483 ms  (t=47.7s)
sessions.admission                             1617 ms  (t=49.7s)
plugins.runtime-post-bind                     12270 ms  (t=69.6s)
sidecars.main-session-recovery                12613 ms  (t=69.9s)
→ http server listening (21 plugins; 46.2s)
post-ready.startup-maintenance                12499 ms  (t=91.1s)
sidecars.subagent-recovery                    15990 ms  (t=94.6s)
```

The same phases at the 2026-10-26 08:59:33 start: `config.auth 24362 ms`, `plugins.runtime-post-bind 17880 ms`, `sidecars.main-session-recovery 25843 ms`, `process.bootstrap 36156 ms`.

During every start there are repeated slow SQLite holds on the state DB:

```
[sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold async=false database=<state>/openclaw.sqlite operation=state.admission.fast-path elapsedMs=2677 …
[sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold async=false database=<state>/openclaw.sqlite operation=cron.history-maintenance elapsedMs=2276 …
[sqlite/transaction] slow SQLite transaction hold async=false database=<agent>/openclaw-agent.sqlite operation=sessions.transcript-index.preflight elapsedMs=1158 …
[session-sqlite] slow SQLite reclamation Worker operation … reclamationKind=canonical-validation … elapsedMs=6480 outcome=resolved   (10-15 start)
```

### Expected

`config.auth` (17 to 24 s) and `plugins.runtime-post-bind` (12 to 18 s) take far longer than their names suggest. I would expect a start under 30 s on a 16-vCPU host with local SQLite.

### Actual

Each restart takes 56 to 125 s of downtime, and recovery sidecars keep running for another 20 to 45 s after the listener is up. Restarts are frequent here: 26 in 16 days, including OOM, update and config reloads. That makes this the most visible availability cost.

## 3. `memory-core-index` plugin service stop timeout breaks `plugins.reload`

### Observed (2026.10.6, 2026-10-26 14:25 to 14:27)

```
[plugins] plugin service degraded (plugin=memory-core, service=memory-core-index): plugin service stop timed out after 4999ms
[ws] ⇄ res ✗ plugins.reload 125478ms errorCode=UNAVAILABLE errorMessage=Plugin operation failed during drain: plugin service replacement cleanup failed | plugin service stop failed (plugin=memory-core, service=memory-core-index): plugin service stop timed out after 4997ms
[ws] ⇄ res ✗ plugins.reload 82526ms errorCode=UNAVAILABLE errorMessage=… plugin service stop failed (plugin=memory-core, service=memory-core-index): plugin service stop timed out …
```

There were 4 failed `plugins.reload` calls (82 to 125 s each). Every one failed on the same service. Afterwards a full gateway restart was needed.

### Expected

The `memory-core-index` stop either finishes within the 5 s budget (it should abort or checkpoint a running index pass), or the reload goes ahead with a degraded memory-core instead of failing the whole operation.

### Actual

The 5 s stop budget expires, and `plugins.reload` fails with `UNAVAILABLE` after 1.5 to 2 minutes of drain. Unrelated plugins can no longer be hot-reloaded while the index is busy.

## Steps to reproduce (best effort)

1. Run the gateway as a systemd unit with 18+ plugins, including `browser`, `codex`, `memory-core`, and CLI-backed agents (`claude`), plus two Telegram accounts and a few hundred cron jobs.
2. Leave it up for 2 to 4 days under normal chat and cron load, with browser tool use and subagent turns.
3. Watch `[diagnostics/memory]`, the systemd `Consumed … memory peak` lines and `systemd-cgls -u openclaw-gateway`. Gateway RSS climbs, and the child-process count under the unit climbs too.
4. For (3), call `plugins.reload` while `memory-core` is indexing.

## Logs and what I can provide

- The full `journalctl -u openclaw-gateway` export for the windows above, redacted, on request. Chat content is logged at info level and would need scrubbing first.
- The kernel OOM report from 2026-10-15 22:15:53 to 22:15:56 (759 lines).
- A heap snapshot or `--trace-warnings` run if you can say how to pass Node flags through `openclaw gateway`.

## Workarounds in place on our side

- systemd `MemoryHigh=12G` / `MemoryMax=16G` on the unit, an OOM policy drop-in and `Restart=always`.
- An external memory-pressure watcher and idle-gated restarts.
- None of these address the root cause.


---
Possibly related (startup part): #155859 (startup wall-time scales with plugin count).

issues.body:
GPT-6 should get the shared OpenClaw instructions without also inheriting the GPT-5 behavior contract and friendly style. [#166152](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166152) deliberately extended that contract to Astra so the default model would receive the same guidance as GPT-5. [#166169](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166169) narrowed the match to generations 5 and 6. This is a request to revisit that decision, not a claim that the matcher is doing something unintended.

## What I observed

In an Astra diagnostic session, the assistant checked one source, found errors that did not explain the reported symptom, and asked me for a session link before trying the available read-only session search. The assembled instructions included “Incomplete until every item handled or [blocked] with missing input.” This is one observed premature handoff, not a controlled comparison proving the overlay caused it.

## Reproducible evidence

On `b22df8b94835e90191a36cf8496ad2cdffee7223`, the [shared provider runtime](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/b22df8b94835e90191a36cf8496ad2cdffee7223/src/plugins/provider-runtime.ts#L157-L178) merges the [legacy overlay](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/b22df8b94835e90191a36cf8496ad2cdffee7223/src/agents/gpt5-prompt-overlay.ts#L92-L116) into OpenClaw-assembled prompts. This can be reproduced from an installed checkout without credentials or a model call.

```js
import { resolveGpt5SystemPromptContribution as overlay } from 'openclaw/plugin-sdk/provider-model-metadata';
for (const modelId of ['gpt-5', 'gpt-6-astra', 'openai/gpt-6.2-astra', 'gpt-6.2-sol', 'gemini-2.5-flash']) {
  const x = overlay({ modelId });
  console.log(modelId, !!x?.stablePrefix?.includes('<completion_contract>'), !!x?.sectionOverrides?.interaction_style);
}
```

Actual output, with the completion contract first and friendly style second

```text
gpt-5 true true
gpt-6-astra true true
openai/gpt-6.2-astra true true
gpt-6.2-sol true true
gemini-2.5-flash false false
```

## Why revisit it for GPT-6

OpenAI’s [GPT-6.2 prompting guide, Task completion](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model#task-completion) says the model may propose a next step and wait, and recommends taking authorized next steps instead of handing routine work back to the user. Its writing guidance also recommends revisiting inherited concision instructions. The [Astra prompting article, Persistence and Decision boundaries](https://developers.openai.com/blog/rethinking-skills-and-prompts-for-gpt-6-astra#persistence) specifically warns that boundaries written for earlier models can make Astra stop where the operator intended it to continue. OpenAI recommends reassessing those instructions. Removing this particular overlay is the proposed OpenClaw change.

## Expected result

Keep GPT-5 unchanged. Fresh OpenClaw-assembled prompts for all `gpt-6*` models, including provider-qualified IDs, should get neither the legacy behavior block nor its friendly style override. Leave shared instructions, approvals, native Codex behavior and other provider contributions alone. Cover bare and routed GPT-6 IDs with a GPT-5 positive control, and update the docs that currently describe GPT-6 as included.

issues.body:
## What happens

In the Control UI, editing only the caption of an already recovered unsent attachment and immediately reloading preserves the edited caption but silently drops the attachment.

## Reproduction

1. Open a connected chat and select a small file through the composer file input.
2. Type a caption, wait five seconds, and reload.
3. Confirm that both the filename and caption were restored.
4. Append only `!` to the caption and immediately reload, within about 10 ms.
5. After reconnection, inspect the composer.

Expected: the previously saved attachment and edited caption remain. Actual: the caption remains, but the attachment disappears without a storage or draft-loss warning.

## Evidence

The supplied real-Gateway reproduction used main `b8c9305ae2271fb0a72191fd37a0445556da4690`, an isolated source-built Gateway, and Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4 on macOS arm64. Each trial used a fresh persistent browser profile and `draft-note.txt` (49 bytes).

| Second reload | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Five immediate reloads, 0.8 to 1.25 ms after the caption edit | 5/5 retained the edited caption and lost the attachment |
| Two controls, about five seconds after the edit | 2/2 retained both |

All seven trials had successfully restored the attachment before the caption-only edit. Two immediate trials used Chrome `Page.reload` after trusted `Input.insertText`, with 2.9 ms and 3 ms measured from input to `beforeunload`. No dialogs, visible loss warnings, or browser errors were recorded.

These results were supplied by a separate test-Gateway run, not reproduced by the filing agent. Beta.3 and stable 2026.11.7 were also reported affected, but were not rechecked in this main run.

## Intended behavior and suspected cause

The [draft recovery documentation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/b8c9305ae2271fb0a72191fd37a0445556da4690/docs/web/control-ui/sessions-and-sidebar.md#L975) says staged attachments are recoverable within the same browser profile and Gateway credential scope. In the [restore owner](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/b8c9305ae2271fb0a72191fd37a0445556da4690/ui/src/pages/chat/durable-composer-persistence.ts#L205-L216), an older durable draft revision is skipped before attachment hydration. A newer synchronous caption revision surviving an interrupted asynchronous draft write is consistent with the failure. Stored revisions were not directly traced in the supplied run.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

An agent on a CLI backend such as `claude-cli` gets the `deep_research` tool through the Gateway's loopback MCP server, and that copy offers only `action: "start" | "capabilities"`. The `status`, `result`, `resume` and `cancel` actions are dropped, so the agent can start a research job but can never read its report or cancel it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Fresh 2026.11.10 profile, main agent on `claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5`, Deep Research left at its default (portable, enabled).
2. Ask the agent: "Do not call deep_research. Load the schema of the deep_research tool and print verbatim, as JSON, the input schema property `action` and the list of top-level property names."
3. Check the Gateway log for `mcp-loopback`.

### Expected behavior

`action` allows all six values from `researchToolSchema` (`extensions/deep-research/src/contract.ts:110`): `start`, `status`, `result`, `resume`, `cancel`, `capabilities`.

### Actual behavior

The agent reports (run twice, same result):

```json
{
  "action": {"enum": ["start", "capabilities"], "type": "string"},
  "topLevelPropertyNames": ["action", "idempotencyKey", "jobId", "request"]
}
```

`jobId` survives, but no action that uses it does. The Gateway logs this on the first tool list:

```
[mcp-loopback] conflicting schema definitions for "deep_research.action", keeping the first variant
```

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.10 (`6ea542fd97e`). Current `main` (`254f6024289`) has the same code in the three files named below.

### Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS

### Install method

npm global

### Model

claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw Gateway -> claude-cli backend (Claude Code 2.1.322) -> Gateway loopback MCP server for OpenClaw tools.

### Additional provider/model setup details

Nothing special: a throwaway test profile with default config. Any CLI backend that receives OpenClaw tools over the loopback MCP server should be affected, since the schema is rewritten there.

### Logs

See Actual behavior. In the same run, `deep_research` was the only tool that logged this warning.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Reproduced on a fresh test profile with no other changes (output above). We did not test the embedded runtime.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: agents on CLI backends (claude-cli and similar) that use Deep Research.
- Severity: blocks the tool's main use. A job can be started but its report can't be read.
- Frequency: always.
- Consequence: wasted research runs, and no way to cancel one from chat.

### Additional information

Related: #201195. That bug stops `deep_research start` itself on claude-cli turns. This one is separate: it decides which actions the agent is offered, and it remains after that fix.

<details>
<summary>Claude Opus 5.5</summary>

Where the actions are lost, at `254f6024289` (same lines in 2026.11.10):

- `researchToolSchema` is a union of three objects. Variant 1 has `action: Literal("start")`, variant 2 has `action: Union([Literal("status"), Literal("result"), Literal("resume"), Literal("cancel")])`, and variant 3 has `action: Literal("capabilities")`. TypeBox emits variant 2's `action` as `{ anyOf: [{ const: "status", type: "string" }, ...] }`.
- `flattenUnionSchema` (`src/gateway/mcp-http.schema.ts:41`) merges the variants' properties for MCP clients. For a repeated key it calls `mergeLiteralSchemas` (`src/shared/json-schema-literals.ts:49`).
- `readLiteralSchemaValues` (`src/shared/json-schema-literals.ts:27`) only reads `const` and `enum`, so it returns `undefined` for the `anyOf` and the merge gives up. `flattenUnionSchema` then logs the warning at line 97 and keeps `{ const: "start" }`. Variant 3 merges normally, so the result is `enum: ["start", "capabilities"]`.

A likely fix (not written or tested): let `readLiteralSchemaValues` treat an `anyOf`/`oneOf` whose members are all literal schemas with matching constraints as their combined values. The constraint comparison in `mergeLiteralSchemas` would also need to read the members' `type` instead of the `anyOf` key. Changing the tool's schema to a flat `stringEnum` for variant 2 would also work, but only for this one tool.

</details>

issues.body:
## Summary

On 2026.9.6 the Gateway's main-isolate heap grows steadily at rest, about 45–100 MiB/h, until it reaches Node's default V8 ceiling (~4.2 GiB on this host) and aborts with `Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit`. It happened once (2026-09-26); without a restart or a larger heap it would recur within about a day.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6, npm global install; Node v24.21.0; Linux x86_64
- Gateway as a `systemd --user` service; 60 GiB RAM; default V8 heap limit reported by Node: 4288 MiB
- 23 configured agents; ~1,470 stored session rows across agents (about +24/day); ~23 enabled cron jobs (daily/weekly)
- Channel: Discord. Plugins include anthropic, openai, codex, discord, memory-core (local embeddings), memory-wiki, browser
- Two small local `--import` module hooks via `NODE_OPTIONS`: one caps rate-limit retry backoff, one maps bare numeric Discord ids to `channel:` targets. They only rewrite a few expressions at load time. They are listed so nothing is hidden, but we have no evidence they are involved.

## Observed

The heap figures come from the Gateway's own `[diagnostics/memory]` samples.

**Crash.** The Gateway ran for 1h49m and then aborted:

```
Mark-Compact (reduce) 4035.1 (4079.5) -> 3987.1 (4047.2) MB ...
FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

That window had many config hot reloads, and growth was faster: ~170 MiB/h or more.

**After a restart (low traffic):**

| Time since start | Heap used |
|---|---|
| 0:21 | 1.48 GiB |
| 2:21 | 2.24 GiB |
| 12:10 | 2.67 GiB |
| 13:41 | 2.91 GiB |

- Between 2:30 and 12:10 there were **no config reloads**, and the heap still grew ~45 MiB/h.
- RSS stays about 2–2.5 GiB above heap used (5–6 GiB total).
- Worker isolates are separate and smaller; for example, `prepared-model-catalog.worker.js` used 94–424 MB.

## Allocation sampling (`diagnostics.heapProfile`)

**Caveat:** this shows the allocation sites of sampled bytes still live at the end of the window, **not retainer paths**. We have not taken a heap snapshot; see the offer below.

**Sample 1** (steady state, heap 2.9 GiB, 30 s):
- 0.87 MB still live. That is about the observed growth rate: 100 MiB/h ≈ 0.85 MB per 30 s.
- 59% (0.51 MB): `deserialize (node:v8)` ← `decodeSqliteWorkerReplyValue` ← `receiveSqliteWorkerReply` ← `receiveReply` (`sqlite-worker-store-*.mjs`).
- 18%: the profiler itself (`node:inspector post`).
- The rest was small: `listPending` (ingress queue), `computeStaggeredCronNextRunAtMs`, host CPU sampling.

**Sample 2** (40 min after restart, heap ~0.65–1 GiB, 30 s, while caches were warming):

| Share | Allocation site |
|---|---|
| 39% | redacted frame ← `(root)` |
| 12% | `materializeSessionRow` ← `readResidentSessionRow` ← `materialize` (`session-row-projection-*.mjs`) |
| 9% | redacted ← `index` ← `put` ← `acquireSessionRowEntry` (`session-row-prepared-read-*.mjs`) |
| 5% | `acquireSessionRowEntry` ← … ← `withAgentRosterFactsBatch` |
| 4% | `readResidentSessionRow` ← `materialize` |

**Session rows alone don't account for it.** Their total stored JSON is ~45 MB and grows ~0.7 MB/day, far below ~1 GB/day of heap growth. If something retains deserialized SQLite reply values, or repeatedly re-materializes rows while keeping the old objects reachable, that would fit both samples. That is a guess, not a finding.

## Related

- #114765 and #89315: earlier at-rest heap growth, closed.
- #129421: closed for lack of a retainer path.
- #157351: 2026.9.6 plugin re-capture and compile-cache growth. We also saw ~390K compile-cache files in tmpfs `/tmp` after a day of frequent hot reloads, which exhausted its inodes.

## Workaround

`--max-old-space-size=10240` as a direct `node` argument in the service's `ExecStart` (not `NODE_OPTIONS`). That buys days; it does not stop the growth.

## Offer

If a retainer path is needed, we can take a heap snapshot on our side and share an **aggregated** summary: constructor names, retained sizes and retainer chains, with no string contents. Raw snapshots would contain private conversation data, so we cannot attach them.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

After upgrading to 2026.11.10, openclaw doctor reports that root MEMORY.md and USER.md for agent main are excluded from automatic context because their memory provenance is untrusted (last tracked write in early November; the files were later edited by the operator on the host and via shell). The docs (concepts/memory-provenance, cli/memory) explain how files become untrusted, but I couldn't find a supported way for the owner to review a file and mark it trusted again. Once untrusted, later owner writes keep it untrusted.

Questions:

Is there a command or UI action to accept the current content as trusted after review, for example openclaw memory trust --agent main --file MEMORY.md?
If not, is it planned? For now we work around it by having the agent read the files explicitly at session start.

Self-hosted, Docker, OpenClaw 2026.11.10 (6ea542f).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Agent "main" running on OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (Docker, self-hosted). Its root MEMORY.md and USER.md had been edited over time both by the agent and from the host shell.
2. Upgrade the gateway to 2026.11.10 (6ea542f) and run `openclaw doctor --fix` (migration), then start the gateway.
3. Run `openclaw doctor`.
   Observed: "Memory provenance" check -> "Agent "main": MEMORY.md is excluded from automatic context: its memory provenance is untrusted. Last recorded tracked write: 2026-11-03T15:20:40.220Z, session agent:main:main." Same for USER.md (last tracked write 2026-11-02T08:02:03.575Z).
4. Start a new main session. Gateway log shows: "excluding MEMORY.md from automatic memory context: memory provenance is untrusted" (and the same for USER.md).
5. Look for a way to restore trust after review (`openclaw memory --help`, `openclaw doctor`, docs concepts/memory-provenance and cli/memory): no command or option found.

### Expected behavior

In 2026.11.7 (the version we ran before upgrading), root MEMORY.md and USER.md for agent "main" were loaded into automatic context on every main session. After upgrading to 2026.11.10 (6ea542f), they are excluded with "memory provenance is untrusted" (per docs: concepts/memory-provenance).

Expected: after the owner reviews the files, there should be a supported way to mark them trusted again (CLI command, doctor fix, or Control UI action), so they return to automatic context. The docs describe how a file becomes untrusted, and say later owner writes keep it untrusted, but describe no way to restore trust.

### Actual behavior

After upgrading to 2026.11.10 (6ea542f), root MEMORY.md and USER.md of agent "main" are no longer included in automatic context.

Evidence:
- `openclaw doctor` -> "Memory provenance" section, under "Fix now":
  "Agent "main": MEMORY.md is excluded from automatic context: its memory provenance is untrusted. Last recorded tracked write: 2026-11-03T15:20:40.220Z, session agent:main:main."
  "Agent "main": USER.md is excluded from automatic context: its memory provenance is untrusted. Last recorded tracked write: 2026-11-02T08:02:03.575Z, session agent:main:main."
  Next step shown: "Review the file content. ... This check reports the exclusion only; it does not change provenance."
- Gateway log on a new main session:
  "[agent/embedded] excluding USER.md from automatic memory context: memory provenance is untrusted; run `openclaw doctor` for the last recorded write"
  "[agent/embedded] excluding MEMORY.md from automatic memory context: memory provenance is untrusted; run `openclaw doctor` for the last recorded write"
- No command, flag or UI action found to mark the reviewed files trusted again (`openclaw memory --help`, `openclaw doctor`, docs concepts/memory-provenance and cli/memory).

A second agent on another gateway with the same version has no excluded files.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.10 (6ea542f)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04 (host), kernel 7.0.0-44; gateway in Docker container

### Install method

docker (custom image based on official image + npm i -g openclaw@2026.11.10)

### Model

openai/gpt-6.1-sol (agent main; not model-specific, the exclusion happens before the model call)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> openai (ChatGPT account auth profile) -> gpt-6.1-sol

### Additional provider/model setup details

Not provider-related: the exclusion happens in automatic context assembly before any model call (memory-core / agent bootstrap).
Agent "main": primary openai/gpt-6.1-sol via ChatGPT account auth profile; fallbacks claude-cli (Sonnet) and deepseek-native/deepseek-flash.
Memory search: memory-core with a local Ollama embedding model (qwen3-embedding 8B).
No proxies or model routers between OpenClaw and the provider.

issues.body:
### Summary

`MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` are the curated roots that get injected into every new session's bootstrap prompt. Their injection is gated by a per-file provenance record (`originClass`). Once that record becomes `"untrusted"`, the file is silently dropped from the bootstrap prompt **forever** — no error, no warning, no log line, no CLI, no self-heal.

The previous version of this report blamed a specific upgrade for introducing the mechanism. **That was wrong** — see "Not a regression" below.

Three independent paths flip a file to `"untrusted"`:

1. **Network-tainted turn (the landmine).** Any write to a curated root made in a turn where *any* tool result came from the network is recorded as `"untrusted"`. **— reproduced 2026-09-20** (a `web_search` result in the same turn poisoned the write of a scratch `memory/*.md` file: recorded `originClass: "untrusted"`).
2. **Out-of-band edit.** Content on disk that no longer matches the last recorded hash; the next tracked write is what actually gets demoted. **— reproduced 2026-09-20** in a controlled three-window experiment.
3. **Non-owner sender.** A write made in a turn whose sender is not the owner. *— read from source only; not reproduced by us.*

All three are permanent (ratchet) and all three are invisible.

### What we reproduced vs. what we read from source

Everything below is traceable either to the shipped `dist/` of the version in use, or to a ledger reading from a live instance. Nothing is speculative.

| Claim | Evidence |
|---|---|
| `originClass` gate exists; only `MEMORY.md` and `USER.md` are candidates | source: `resolveIneligibleAutomaticMemoryFiles()` filters on `file.name === DEFAULT_MEMORY_FILENAME \|\| file.name === "USER.md"` |
| The write-time classification is a ratchet | source: the ternary quoted below, read verbatim |
| Egress-time `untrusted` from taint / non-owner | source: `resolveOriginClass`, plus the taint observer (`resultContentSource === "network"`) |
| A network-tainted turn poisons the write | **reproduced** live (see path 1 above) |
| An out-of-band edit + the next tracked write kills the file | **reproduced** live, with ledger readings at each step |
| The symptom is silent (no warning/log/CLI) | observed across ~3 days on a live instance; `doctor` never surfaced it |
| Not a regression introduced by our upgrade | 2026.8.1 and 2026.9.4 packages diffed: identical code paths |

### Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.4 (3a9d69d)** (observed in production); identical code paths verified present in **2026.8.1**
- Node v24.21.0, Linux x64
- `memory-core` bundled plugin (default), workspace files backend

### Not a regression

The mechanism exists identically in **2026.8.1** — verified by diffing the two installed packages:

| artifact | 2026.8.1 | 2026.9.4 |
|---|---|---|
| `memory-artifact-provenance` | present | present |
| `memory-path-provenance` | present | present |
| write-time classification expression | identical | identical |
| bootstrap injection gate | identical | identical |

Both versions wire it into `workspace-path-classifier`. So nothing about an upgrade introduced this; it simply had not been *observed* before.

### Mechanism

**Write-time record** (`src/memory/memory-artifact-provenance.ts`):

```ts
const originClass =
  params.originClass === "agent" &&
  (!previous || (previous.originClass === "agent" && previous.fileHash === sha256(params.contentBefore)))
    ? "agent"
    : "untrusted";
```

**Where `params.originClass` comes from** — this is the part the docs don't spell out:

```ts
resolveOriginClass: () =>
  options?.senderIsOwner === false || options?.isTurnTainted?.() === true
    ? "untrusted"
    : "agent",
```

and taint is defined as:

```ts
function createAgentTurnTaintState(initiallyTainted = false) {
  let tainted = initiallyTainted;
  return {
    observe(observation) {
      if (!observation.presentationOnly && observation.resultContentSource === "network") tainted = true;
    },
    isTainted: () => tainted,
  };
}
```

So a turn becomes tainted the moment any non-presentation tool result is network-sourced — i.e. **`web_search` / `web_fetch` poison every curated-root write made later in that same turn.**

**Read-time gate** (`extensions/memory-core/src/memory/memory-path-provenance.ts`):

```ts
const recorded = isWorkspaceMemory ? await readMemoryArtifactProvenance({ ... }) : undefined;
if (recorded) return { curatedRoot, originClass: recorded.originClass };
return { curatedRoot, originClass: isWorkspaceMemory ? "agent" : "untrusted" };
```

Note the fallback: **no record ⇒ `"agent"` (eligible)**. This is why deleting the row restores injection.

### Steps to reproduce (path 1 — no user misbehavior required)

1. Fresh workspace; write `MEMORY.md` via agent tools → record `originClass: "agent"`.
2. In a later turn: call `web_search` (or `web_fetch`) and then write `MEMORY.md` **in the same turn** via agent tools.
3. The write is recorded as `originClass: "untrusted"` — the turn was tainted and `resolveOriginClass()` returned `"untrusted"`, which short-circuits the whole expression.
4. From the next run on, `MEMORY.md` is excluded from the bootstrap prompt for every session. Retrieval, disk content, and the memory index all still look healthy.
5. Every subsequent write to that file re-records `"untrusted"`, forever.

### Steps to reproduce (path 3 — the classic out-of-band edit)

1. Agent writes `MEMORY.md` → `originClass: "agent"`, `fileHash: hash(v1)`.
2. Owner edits the file directly (any editor / external process). No record update.
3. Agent writes `MEMORY.md` again later. `previous.fileHash === sha256(contentBefore)` fails → new record `"untrusted"`.
4. Same silent exclusion from then on.

### Field evidence (a real instance, timestamps in UTC+8)

Provenance store for one workspace: 35 records dating back to 2026-08-31 — so the chain was live long before anyone suspected anything. Eight files were already `"untrusted"` when we went looking, including several daily memory files.

| file | demoted at | recorded session |
|---|---|---|
| `USER.md` | 2026-09-08 20:45:05 | `agent:main:node-…` |
| `MEMORY.md` | 2026-09-14 09:48:41 | `agent:main:dashboard:…` |

Other `"untrusted"` files: six `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` dailies, plus two more files poisoned by the ratchet afterwards.

The user-visible symptom (missing bootstrap memory) only became apparent once `MEMORY.md` itself was hit — `USER.md` had been silently degraded for six days without anyone noticing. **It had been firing all along; there was simply nothing watching.**

### Why it never recovers

- Ratchet: once `previous.originClass` is `"untrusted"`, `previous.originClass === "agent"` can never hold again, so every later write re-records `"untrusted"` — even content-identical writes, even through the proper tool path.
- The read-time fallback to `"agent"` only applies when **no record exists**.
- No user-facing surface: `openclaw memory` has no provenance subcommand; `openclaw doctor` does not report exclusions; the `warn` callback in the exclusion path never reaches the user.
- Bonus trap: the internal `main` lane does not consume root memory at all, so testing with it yields a **false negative** — you can "verify" that everything is fine while every interactive session is memory-less.

### Impact

- The agent wakes with no `MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` — i.e. no long-term memory anchor, no persona continuity, no operating rules — while every health signal says the system is fine.
- The trigger set includes **normal, encouraged behavior** (searching the web before writing memory) and **legitimate owner workflow** (editing one's own memory file).
- In our instance it silently persisted across days and was reported by the user only as "something feels off".

### Recovery (current workaround)

Manual surgery on the gateway state DB:

```sql
DELETE FROM plugin_state_entries
WHERE plugin_id = 'core:memory-artifact-provenance'
  AND namespace = 'workspace-files'
  AND entry_key = '<workspaceKey>:<sha256(relativePath)>';
```

then force a memory re-index (deleting the row alone leaves the already-built index chunks marked untrusted):

```bash
openclaw memory index --force
```

After that, classification falls back to `"agent"` and bootstrap injection resumes. Verified end-to-end: a fresh interactive session regained its bootstrap memory.

### Suggestions

1. **Observability — highest value.** Surface exclusions. `openclaw doctor` should print e.g. `MEMORY.md excluded from bootstrap: provenance=untrusted, observed 2026-09-14`, and the existing `warn` in the exclusion path should reach the user/log instead of being swallowed.
2. **CLI.** Add `openclaw memory provenance list|reset [--agent <id>]` — list `workspace-files` records per workspace, and reset one or more files (delete the row so classification falls back to `"agent"`).
3. **Soften the ratchet.** For curated roots, a subsequent clean agent write should be able to re-attest to `"agent"` rather than being permanently poisoned. Alternatively, an out-of-band owner edit on a curated root should be classified `"owner"` (already an accepted source by the injection eligibility check) rather than `"untrusted"`.
4. **Distinguish taint from distrust.** A *network-tainted* write is not the same threat as a *foreign writer*. At minimum, tainting should not permanently demote a curated root written by the owner's own agent; consider recording the taint as a separate field instead of overloading `originClass`.
5. **Docs.** Document (a) the three paths into `"untrusted"`, (b) that `"" ⇒ agent""` for a missing record, and (c) the false-negative trap: a non-interactive `main`-lane session doesn't consume root memory, so it must not be used to verify injection.

issues.body:
**Status: implementation published in draft PR [#205791](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205791).** The bounded Control UI path is implemented with partial verification. Mandatory browser/device qualification, required CI and maintainer design acceptance remain open; this issue stays open and its acceptance boxes remain unchecked.


## Summary

Add semantic formatting to intelligent dictation so a user can speak a short list, a sequence of steps or paragraph breaks and receive readable structure in the destination's supported format. The same spoken content should become plain text in a basic field, Markdown in an explicitly Markdown-capable target, or sanitized rich text where a qualified insertion adapter supports it. Content must remain identical in meaning across renderers.

## Problem to solve

The feature audit found no direct open item covering this general formatting contract. Current microphone/recording PRs concern capture or gestures and must not be treated as an implementation of lists or paragraphs. This proposal addresses structure, not improving the user's argument, changing tone or generating content that was never spoken.

## Proposed solution

### Scope and ownership

M11 (companion design proposal) owns refinement and validation. M04 produces a bounded semantic document representation and deterministic renderings. M10 (companion design proposal) reports target capabilities and performs the insertion; M04 does not need M10 implemented to test its pure renderer. M01 (companion design proposal) handles punctuation, M05 (companion design proposal) selects allowed style/formatting preferences, and M08 (companion design proposal) protects code.

Initial structures: paragraphs, line breaks, unordered lists and ordered lists. Explicit headings may be added if the first acceptance scope includes them. Tables, spreadsheet cells, formulas, executable commands, attachments, automatic links, embedded media and application-specific document automation are excluded. A spoken URL can remain text; this feature must not fetch it. Checklists may render as plain textual markers only when selected, not as interactive task objects.

### Required behavior and examples

1. Offer **Preserve**, **Explicit structure**, and an optional **Suggest structure** mode. Preserve keeps the recognizer's structure. Explicit structure interprets enabled phrases such as “new paragraph,” “bullet,” and “next item.” Suggest structure may propose a list but requires review when the change depends on interpreting the speaker's intention.
2. Select a renderer from actual target capabilities, not an application-name guess. If capability is absent, unsupported or stale, fall back to readable plain text. Never paste raw HTML into a text field while reporting rich-text success.
3. Preserve item order, item count, nested content within the agreed depth limit, explicit numbering, quantities, names and negation. Do not manufacture a list item to make a sequence symmetrical or silently restart numbering when the user said “step three.”
4. Interpret formatting commands only outside literal/quoted/code ranges and only in the selected grammar. `The phrase new paragraph appears in the instructions` must retain those words in normal prose.
5. Keep one semantic content source for all renderings. Validation should compare source-token coverage and structure before rendering; renderer-specific escaping must not rewrite meaning.
6. Sanitize rich text through an allowlist and explicit serialization. Model output must never supply executable HTML, script, event handlers, CSS, remote resources or arbitrary clipboard MIME types.

#### Authored fixtures

| Speech and selected policy | Prepared result |
| --- | --- |
| `Shopping list bullet milk next item eggs next item rice` in Explicit structure | A three-item list in the spoken order. Plain text uses readable line markers; Markdown uses list syntax; qualified rich text uses list nodes. |
| `First check power second restart the app` in Suggest structure | A reviewable two-step candidate; no automatic deletion of `first`/`second` if the structure is uncertain. |
| `Opening paragraph new paragraph closing paragraph` in Explicit structure | Two paragraphs with predictable spacing in each renderer. |
| `Do not enable auto renew bullet review the invoice` | Preserve the prohibition; do not move `not` into a lost heading or list marker. |
| `The words bullet and next item are examples` in Preserve | Keep the words as prose. |
| Text containing `*`, `_`, brackets, `<script>` and code literals | Escape/render safely; no code execution, link fetch or accidental formatting of protected strings. |
| Unsupported target or a changed target before commit | Plain-text/review fallback through M10; no silent incompatible insertion. |

These fixtures are proposed expected behavior, not screenshots or measured product output.

### Proposed representation and validation

Use a small versioned document value carried by the accepted M11 result type. Conceptually it contains an ordered sequence of paragraph/list blocks, bounded text runs, source-span references and optional protected-literal annotations. This is proposed structure, not a committed API. Prefer extending an existing safe representation if source inspection identifies a suitable owner; do not introduce a full document editor framework for four block types.

Suggested initial limits are 100 blocks, 100 list items, nesting depth 3 and the M11 text-size limit. The exact limits need corpus and UI qualification. Validation rejects cycles, unknown node types, invalid source ranges, duplicate/lost content, oversized depth and empty structural artifacts that have no semantic purpose. A rejected structure falls back to the validated plain textual candidate, preserving the user's words.

Structural transforms must reference the original transcript through the shared source map. Accepted spoken formatting markers can be consumed with explicit reason records; other lexical tokens cannot disappear. Correction and filler cleanup may change content only through their own accepted semantic plan before rendering. Do not ask each renderer to perform a second semantic rewrite.

For Markdown, use a declared syntax profile and test against that parser. CommonMark specifies block/inline structure and escaping, but it is not a universal contract for every host application's Markdown dialect [source S2]. The first implementation should support the small common subset and show plain text when the target's expectations are unknown. Rich-text output should contain only permitted block/text nodes produced by deterministic serialization.

### Target capability and insertion boundary

The prepared result may include multiple deterministic representations derived from the same document: plain text, declared Markdown and qualified rich text. M10 selects only a representation supported by the live target snapshot and rechecks target identity before commit. A later focus change cannot make the model's remembered app context authoritative.

Plain text is always available. A browser application's rich editor may still require platform-specific proof for undo, selection replacement and paste handling; renderer unit tests do not qualify that adapter. On mobile, the field/keyboard path may support fewer structures. Feature documentation must distinguish “can prepare formatted text” from “can insert rich text into this application.”

Formatting does not press Enter to submit a chat or create a new spreadsheet row. A newline is content only when the adapter can insert it safely. If the target consumes Enter as an action and cannot accept a newline transaction, offer a review/copy route or a single-line rendering selected by the user, not simulated submission keys.

### Configuration and recovery

Recommended defaults: Preserve for existing installations; Explicit structure inside an opt-in intelligent-dictation profile; Suggest structure off initially. Plain text is the safe unknown-target default. Save a formatting policy, permitted block types and optional target/profile override through the common preference owner. Do not store extracted content or a second formatting history.

The effective policy and target-capability revision are fixed for a preparation. A user changes the policy by explicitly reprocessing the unsent draft. That invalidates previous renderings and their insertion eligibility. If the user manually edits prepared text, preserve that edit; do not regenerate structure on every keystroke.

On model failure, structural rejection or unavailable rendering, retain a plain-text draft with a clear status. A rich-text failure after an uncertain insertion must follow M10's at-most-once recovery rules; it cannot immediately retry plain text and risk duplication. Copying a candidate is an explicit user action with normal clipboard behavior, not a hidden fallback that overwrites the user's clipboard.

### Accessibility, privacy and performance

Expose structure in the preview with actual semantic lists/headings where supported, readable labels and keyboard navigation. Offer a text-equivalent preview so users can inspect what will arrive in a plain field. Screen readers should announce structural summaries and changes without reading every streaming render. High contrast and large text layouts must keep fallback/review controls visible.

Only already-admitted transcript/context reaches the structural planner. Rich rendering cannot load network resources, and telemetry must not include document text or clipboard payloads. Field capabilities are a bounded enum/descriptor, not a reason to capture the entire destination document.

Proposed, unmeasured target: deterministic validation plus all enabled renderings should complete within 50 ms p95 for 10,000 characters/100 blocks on agreed desktop hardware. Use iterative/bounded traversal or enforce depth before recursion. Model work shares M11's deadline; rendering must not add another provider call. Benchmark escaped worst cases and repeated nested markers, not just a three-item list.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **M04-AC01:** Policy modes and existing-default preservation work as documented.
- [ ] **M04-AC02:** Paragraph/list fixtures preserve item count/order, numbers, negation and protected text across representations.
- [ ] **M04-AC03:** Literal formatting phrases remain text outside the explicit grammar; suggested structure is reviewable.
- [ ] **M04-AC04:** The bounded document validator rejects invalid/oversized/unknown structures and preserves plain text.
- [ ] **M04-AC05:** Markdown escaping and rich-text sanitization prevent executable content, remote resources and unintended semantics.
- [ ] **M04-AC06:** Target capabilities and revision determine rendering; unknown/stale capabilities do not claim rich-text support.
- [ ] **M04-AC07:** Cancellation, user edits and uncertain insertion do not trigger stale rewrites or duplicate fallback insertion.
- [ ] **M04-AC08:** Formatting never submits the destination, executes commands or creates attachments.
- [ ] **M04-AC09:** Semantic and plain preview modes pass keyboard/screen-reader/large-text qualification.
- [ ] **M04-AC10:** Settings migration, privacy/route preservation and measured resource bounds are documented.

### Platform and offline boundary

The transform contract is independent of OS insertion. A desktop, web or mobile client may expose it only through its qualified M11 request/review path; external-field insertion still depends on M10. A headless caller receives a text/result value, not desktop control. Initial support must name actual tested clients and locales rather than imply universal availability.

Deterministic operations may continue offline when recognized text is already available. Model-assisted behavior follows the selected route and locality policy. If the required route is unavailable, retain available recognized text and disclose the missing refinement; do not silently use a cloud service. This does not promise offline speech recognition or recover words a recognizer never returned.

## Alternatives considered

Always emitting Markdown would expose syntax in incompatible targets. Sending formatting keystrokes would couple semantic layout to fragile focus and shortcut assumptions. Allowing arbitrary generated HTML would make validation and safe rendering harder. A small semantic document with capability-selected deterministic renderers provides a bounded initial scope.

## Impact

Users would receive readable paragraphs and lists where the destination supports them, with a plain-text fallback. The rollout would preserve the spoken content and avoid assuming that a new line is safe in every target. Claimed rich-text formats require separate compatibility evidence.

## Evidence/examples

The examples below remain acceptance fixtures. [Draft PR #205791](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205791) provides implementation, focused regression and measured performance evidence; actual browser/device qualification remains blocked or not run as individually documented there. Tracker observations are bounded research, not proof that a capability is absent.

### Verification and rollout

Use golden semantic documents and authored speech fixtures; compare both parser output and plain-text meaning. Fuzz delimiters, Unicode boundaries, nesting, block count, malicious HTML and malformed source maps. Round-trip tests should not merely compare the serializer with itself: parse using the declared independent syntax implementation and assert structural/content invariants.

Exercise one plain field, one declared Markdown field and one qualified rich editor through actual insertion. Record exact OS/application versions, undo behavior and focus-change refusal. A microphone-to-list test should separate recognition, planning, rendering and insertion evidence. Run cases with cleanup/correction enabled to prove shared source maps remain correct.

Land the representation and pure renderers on M11 first; enable Explicit structure on one supported surface; add rich adapters only after M10 qualification. Rollback disables structure and retains validated plain text. Maintainers must choose the initial block set, Markdown profile and rich-text serialization owner. Recommended choices are no automatic rich-text guessing, no arbitrary HTML, and plain-text fallback with no hidden resubmission.

### Sources and search record

- [Open issue search](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues?q=is%3Aopen+dictation+formatting) and [open PR search](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pulls?q=is%3Aopen+dictation+formatting), checked November 25, 2026. Matches such as microphone gesture/background-recording changes are adjacent, not evidence for semantic formatting; repeat before filing.
- **S2:** [CommonMark 0.31.2 specification](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.31.2/), read November 25, 2026. Used as a declared Markdown reference, not an assertion that every target implements that version.
- [Unicode text segmentation](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/) supplies the source-range boundary reference.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Published as [draft PR #205791](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205791), from `CompleteDotTech:feat/dictation-semantic-formatting` at `75070f7628a8651907294c60ce33037e08be1c85`, based on upstream `04b854b239cd8ab8a14beae4914ed9c54d791e62`. Maintainer edits are enabled. The published tree exactly matches the reviewed local implementation; the default branch was not changed.

## Additional information

Suggested label: `enhancement`. Local IDs in this package are planning references, not GitHub issue numbers. The exact API/config names and implementation base require maintainer review; the intended behavior, defaults and outstanding decisions are documented above.


## Current source inspection and review decisions

The current composer already owns transcription capture (`ComposerDictationSession`), ordered finalization (`ComposerDictationCommits`), and draft insertion (`ComposerDictationOwner`). Bounded live searches on November 25, 2026 did not find an equivalent semantic-formatting implementation or accepted M11 source-map contract. Adjacent capture/recovery PRs #204107, #204287, #198845 and #196063 are not formatting parents. Punctuation proposal #205630 is adjacent; this contribution will not add punctuation/correction or a second provider request.

The concrete implementation proposal extends the existing Control UI owner with a private final-transcript preparation and review boundary, immutable source references, deterministic English explicit-structure grammar, and allowlisted plain/Markdown/HTML preparation. Preserve remains the default; opt-in structure is reviewed before applying to the owned composer. Existing provider selection, capture, account/session ownership and insertion remain authoritative. The SDK was considered; its current composer-task draft proposals do not expose this microphone finalization/source-reference boundary. No new public RPC, plugin export, transcript store, or external application controller is proposed.

**Review decisions requested before acceptance:** confirm the private composer boundary and future M11 integration; the versioned browser-local policy within the existing UI preference owner; English command grammar; paragraph/line-break/ordered/unordered blocks; Markdown profile; and measured text/block/item/depth bounds. These are review proposals, not claimed maintainer approvals. Optional inferred structure, headings, tables and document automation are outside this initial implementation.

Preparing safe rich text is separate from qualifying external rich insertion. M10 adapter qualification, real microphone/STT, assistive-technology operation and target undo/focus evidence will be reported individually. Any unavailable proof or acceptance remains a visible blocker, with the issue left open and the PR draft where permitted.

## Published implementation and remaining qualification

The PR includes the private existing-owner lifecycle integration, bounded semantic document, conservative English explicit grammar, deterministic plain/Markdown/allowlisted-HTML preparation, reviewed capability-gated placement, versioned browser-local opt-in, recovery controls, documentation and focused tests. Rich HTML is preparation/preview only; no native rich insertion adapter is claimed.

Combined local evidence covers 295 distinct passing cases across 13 suites (not one clean 295-case run), supported narrow formatter types and scoped static checks. Warm validation plus rendering p95 met the proposed 50 ms budget for all three measured workloads; full preparation did not meet that threshold for every workload. The PR links the full acceptance ledger, source-bound manifest, logs and recovery patch/bundle.

All ten pull-request workflow runs are currently `action_required`. GitHub explicitly displays **10 workflows awaiting approval** and requires a maintainer; the main CI run has no jobs, and `openclaw/ci-gate` is expected. This supplies no passing build/test CI evidence. Full UI types and production build were resource-blocked locally; pinned Chromium installation returned HTTP 403, so the browser suite executed no scenarios. Actual microphone/STT, browser plain/Markdown insertion and Undo, qualified rich insertion/Undo, screen reader, 400% browser zoom, current-build visuals, production downgrade and speech-route/egress evidence remain open.

The [automated issue review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/205634#issuecomment-7178200686) requests a bounded private prototype and decisions on shared preparation/preference ownership. It is not human maintainer acceptance. The PR cross-links the parallel punctuation/cleanup drafts; consolidation and enabled-together evidence remain pending. Keep this issue open and PR #205791 draft until mandatory qualification and design decisions are established.

## Summary

On Windows 11, `openclaw update --tag 2026.11.5-beta.4 --yes` from a working `2026.11.5-beta.2` install completed candidate validation but failed at `package-swap`:

```text
global-install-failed
package-swap — Exit code: 1; Baseline package scan failed | Package rollback tree changed during verification
Failing check package-swap (baseline-scan-failed) at dist/package-update-steps-Bo7kLWQq.mjs:1936:21
```

The install remained on beta.2. This is not the #200184 `validating` CPU hang; the pipeline reached `Phase: finished` and recorded a structured failure.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200 x64, PowerShell 5.1 over SSH
- Node v26.13.1, npm 11.20.0
- From: `2026.11.5-beta.2 (c0f42f6)`, Scheduled Task gateway running
- Target: `2026.11.5-beta.4`
- Install root: `%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\openclaw`
- No model configured; onboarding used `--auth-choice skip`

## Timeline

- `requested` — 129.26s, package-install succeeded (103.2s)
- `staging` — 29ms
- `validating` — 885.66s
  - `updater-runtime-retention` — 338.82s, 44,776 entries / ~692 MB
  - `candidate-state-snapshot` — 9.77s
  - `candidate-doctor` — 69.17s
  - `candidate-doctor-lint` — 30.27s, 0 errors / 16 warnings, 15 inspections deferred
  - `candidate-config`, `candidate-plugins`, `candidate-recovery`, `candidate-gateway-startup` — all passed
  - `candidate-state-cleanup` — 78ms
- `package-swap` — failed with `baseline-scan-failed`

Failure report:

- `%OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR%\logs\support\openclaw-update-failure-e3512da8_6861_4feb_a461_f266392c64ff.json`
- Result run ID: `ca1bea3c-a5a1-40b6-8031-956685f1729d`
- Before/after version: both `2026.11.5-beta.2`
- Recovery: `serviceRestartSafe: true`, version `2026.11.5-beta.2`

Triage then started but timed out:

```text
Triage could not complete: Triage stopped (timeout).
```

Retained runtime left at:

```text
%TEMP%\openclaw-update-runtime-gmJBxZ
```

`[infra:temp-artifacts] Runtime retained ... cleanup deferred to the next eligible update or openclaw doctor --fix`
## Context

- The machine had a prior `--channel dev` switch attempt that was manually aborted during retained-runtime materialization and cleaned up before this beta test. The beta.2 install then succeeded.
- The failure says the rollback tree changed during verification; possible causes include residual updater runtimes, antivirus scanning, or concurrent writes. The exact `baseline-scan-failed` location is `dist/package-update-steps-Bo7kLWQq.mjs:1936:21`.
- A direct `npm install -g openclaw@2026.11.5-beta.4` was not attempted on this host after the failure.

## Related

- #156023 — closed: npm update fails reproducibly at global install swap (`global-install-failed`)
- #156112 — closed: update fails at global install swap while direct npm install succeeds
- #153014 — closed: hardcoded 30s scan limit in rollback integrity check on slow hardware
- #200676 — open: beta.4 update failure, gateway-recovery-verification
