prs.title: fix(gateway): recover container startup after a crash
prs.body:
Closes #203932

## What Problem This Solves

After a Gateway container is killed, a new Gateway on the same persistent volume cannot inspect the old PID from its new PID namespace. Before this change it waited about 95 seconds and then failed with `GatewayLockNamespaceError` even when the old Gateway was gone, and the only way out was the manual `openclaw gateway recover-lock` procedure.

## User Impact

- Restarting the same container (default container-ID hostname) after SIGKILL takes over immediately.
- A replacement container after SIGKILL takes over once the old owner's heartbeat has been stale for more than 90 seconds, within the existing 95-second wait.
- A still-running Gateway in another container keeps the lock. The contender fails after the same bounded wait as before, and its restart policy can retry.
- Non-container installs keep native PID checks; nothing changes for a single Gateway on one host.
- The confirmed SQLite/PostgreSQL `recover-lock` backend stays available as a hidden diagnostic and is no longer advertised in startup, update, or daemon guidance.

## Why This Change Was Made

Filesystem locks, persisted Gateway owner leases, and SQLite/Doctor admission now share one classification. A different Linux PID namespace counts as dead if (a) the record's hostname is the current container's 12-hex default hostname inside a container, or (b) the lock's heartbeat (sidecar mtime, renewed every 15 seconds) is more than 90 seconds old. The Gateway owner lease now records the same 15-second heartbeat interval so lease age agrees with the file lock. Wait bounds, cancellation, and refusal types match the base.

Accepted edge cases, with no added code: a container paused for more than 90 seconds can resume next to its replacement until its next restart, because this change adds no self-fencing (SQLite's native locking still protects the database file). Two different containers given the same custom 12-hex hostname on one volume would be treated as the same container. Production/docs: +139/−176. Tests: +129/−70.

## Error surfaces

Full diff against merge-base `90ba7624dbdd`. Each row is a new or changed failure path. "Healthy" means a single Gateway, or a normal update, on one host.

| Path | Fires when healthy? | Rollback/outage risk | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Foreign-namespace owner classified **dead** (container hostname or heartbeat over 90 s) | No. Same-namespace owners never take this branch | No new refusal. It removes one. The risk is overlap after a pause of more than 90 s (accepted above) | Kept: this is the fix |
| Wait on a foreign-namespace owner (`acquireGatewayLock`) | No | Same 95 s bound and `GatewayLockError` as base. Only the log text changed | Kept as base. An earlier head waited without limit; removed in `2505c29` and `ac69712` |
| Doctor admission `signal.throwIfAborted()` in `assertCurrent` | — | Would have been a new throw inside Doctor/update admission | **Removed** (`2505c29`). Only the removed unbounded wait needed it |
| Unparseable owner record now threw `GatewayLockNamespaceError` instead of contention | Only with a malformed record | Changed Doctor's retry and the update failure class | **Removed** (`2505c29`). Contention handling is the same as base |
| Projection lock (`gateway.state.lock`) reclaim: unknown owner returns "not stale" instead of throwing | No. The state owner is acquired first | Same outcome (startup fails with `GatewayLockError`), different message | Kept: equivalent and removes a duplicate classifier call |
| Doctor restoration reservation no longer passes its path to the stale check | No | Linux unchanged. Only a namespace-less Windows/macOS reservation (written when boot identity was unavailable) loses heartbeat-based reclaim | Kept: reservations don't renew their mtime, so heartbeat age must not make a live one look dead |
| `hasVerifiedLiveSqliteOwner` returns false for a dead-classified owner | No | Fewer throws. A paused foreign owner may be read as offline | Kept: consistent with the fix |
| Gateway owner lease heartbeat 100 s → 15 s; lease state uses heartbeat age across namespaces | No refusal | More frequent lease writes. A live older (pre-change) Gateway in another container can look "dead" in the lease between 90 and 100 s, but its 15 s file-lock heartbeat still excludes takeover | Kept: required so a live lease isn't judged stale |
| `gateway recover-lock` hidden; `--json` drops `command`; guidance text in legacy-lock, update-refusal, and daemon-diagnostic messages | — | Text/visibility only. No new exit or refusal | Kept |

No new throw, exit, refusal, rollback trigger, or tightened validation remains in Gateway startup or update/Doctor admission.

## Evidence (exact head `ac69712a4729`)

All runs used private rootless Podman 5.7.0 (task-owned `--root/--runroot`, `--network none`, `--http-proxy=false` for builds) and synthetic config/state. The candidate is the npm package built from `ac69712a4729` with `scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs` (build-info commit `ac69712a4729d751…`, buildId `2026.11.10-ac69712a4729-2026-11-26T05-55-50.847Z`).

- **update.run through Doctor admission, systemd user unit (non-container service path):** Debian bookworm + systemd, Node 24.22.3. Published `openclaw@2026.11.10` was installed globally and run as `openclaw-gateway.service` via `openclaw gateway install`. `update.run` targeted the candidate through a loopback registry fixture. For the updater, the candidate's package version was relabeled to 2026.11.11; dist and build-info commit/buildId are unchanged. The run ended `succeeded/finished` in 106 s (recorded downtime 52 s). Ledger: `candidate-admission` ok, `service-stop` ok, `openclaw doctor` exit 0 (`maintenance.begin 0.6 s`, `schema-admission 0.1 s`), `post-update verification` ok. After the update the service reported the candidate buildId with `/healthz` 200, `/readyz` 200, and authenticated `health` RPC ok.
- **Normal restarts of that service:** `openclaw gateway restart` served again in 11 s, `systemctl --user restart` in 9 s, and SIGKILL of MainPID (systemd restart) in 13 s. Each came back with the same buildId, a new bootId, and healthz/readyz/health RPC ok. The unit journal had 0 ownership refusals.
- **Container cells, official image entrypoint (`tini` → `docker-entrypoint.mjs` → Doctor → Gateway), shared named volume:**
  - Same-container SIGKILL restart: ready plus health RPC in 17/18 s, with no wait logged.
  - Replacement container after SIGKILL: waited on the heartbeat and reached ready plus health in 100/101 s.
  - Contender beside a live holder: exited 1 after 98 s. The holder stayed `/readyz` 200 with health RPC ok throughout.
  - After the holder's graceful stop, the contender restarted and was ready in 17 s.
  - One-off `doctor --fix` beside a live Gateway: bounded refusal after 97 s (`cannot verify Gateway ownership`). The serving Gateway was unaffected.
  - Graceful restart: ready in 15/16 s.
- **Container image upgrade:** a published 2026.11.10 image Gateway was SIGKILLed. The candidate on the same volume completed Doctor and was ready plus health in 102/103 s. Config SHA-256 and the persisted disabled cron job were unchanged. All fixture containers and volumes were removed.
- [Hosted CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205709/checks) runs on this head.

Unit tests cover additional rows but are not counted as proof here. These are covered only by unit tests: macOS/Windows legacy namespace-less locks, custom-hostname containers, a paused container overlapping its replacement, PostgreSQL lease recovery, mixed-version lease ages, and the restoration-reservation path.

<details>
<summary>Redacted terminal capture (exact head)</summary>

```text
# systemd user unit, update.run
[+27s] baseline serving: version 2026.11.10 commit 6ea542f healthz 200 readyz 200 healthRpc true
[+29s] run running requested
[+42s] run running validating
[+120s] run running verifying
[+130s] run succeeded finished
[+133s] after update (106s): version 2026.11.11 commit ac69712 buildId 2026.11.10-ac69712a4729-2026-11-26T05-55-50.847Z healthz 200 readyz 200 healthRpc true
[+144s] cli-restart: serving again in 11s
[+153s] systemctl-restart: serving again in 9s
[+166s] sigkill: serving again in 13s (NRestarts 1)
[+166s] ownership refusals in unit journal: 0

# container cells
[+45s] same-container-sigkill: /readyz 200 in 17s, authenticated health RPC OK in 18s
[+153s] replacement-after-sigkill: /readyz 200 in 100s, authenticated health RPC OK in 101s
waiting for the previous Gateway to stop (last heartbeat 13s ago)
[+251s] entrypoint contender beside live holder: exit 1 after 98s; holder /readyz 200
[+269s] contender-restart-after-holder-graceful-stop: /readyz 200 in 17s
[+366s] one-off Doctor beside live Gateway: exit 1 after 97s
[+366s] serving Gateway still ready after Doctor: 200
[+383s] graceful-restart: /readyz 200 in 15s
[+503s] upgrade-after-sigkill (published 2026.11.10 -> candidate): /readyz 200 in 102s, health RPC OK in 103s
└  Doctor complete.
[+504s] upgrade preserved config bytes and the disabled cron job
remaining containers: 0; volumes: 0
```

</details>

prs.title: fix: let memory indexing finish for large PostgreSQL chat histories
prs.body:
Closes #201571
Fixes #205537

## What Problem This Solves

On an agent store moved to PostgreSQL, `openclaw memory index --agent <id>` fails with `ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY` when the agent has a long session history. The same agent indexes fine on SQLite. Memory search for that agent can't be rebuilt.

## User Impact

User impact: memory indexing on PostgreSQL agent stores now completes for large session histories instead of exhausting the 512 MB transcript worker heap. SQLite continues to stream rows within its existing byte budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Large transcripts are read in short slices after the batch transaction. PostgreSQL was excluded from that path because `iterateSqliteQuerySync` buffers a full PostgreSQL result, and the slice query had no SQL bound, so the byte budget could only stop iteration after the whole remainder was already transferred. The PostgreSQL export therefore loaded every row at once.

This change:
- caps each PostgreSQL slice query at 256 rows and resumes after a full page. The existing 2 MiB decoded-byte budget can end a slice early. SQLite keeps its streaming query.
- removes the PostgreSQL exceptions in the export reader and the memory worker's batch sizing, so PostgreSQL defers large transcripts exactly as SQLite does.

The heap cap itself is left alone: per the issue review, raising it only postpones the failure while the read stays unbounded.

Risk: PostgreSQL exports above the 4 MiB retained-snapshot limit now use several short read-only transactions instead of one. Transcript changes between slices are detected by the existing context-version check and retried, same as SQLite.

## Evidence

**End-to-end: shipped `openclaw memory index` on a large PostgreSQL history, unchanged 512 MB worker limit.**

Setup: PostgreSQL 17.12 with `unaccent` and `pg_trgm`. Fresh isolated state with `database.engine: "postgres"` and keyword-only memory (`memory.search.provider: "none"`), because native Windows can't run `database port` yet. One agent `main` with one long DM session: 30,000 messages of 8 KiB each, 30,001 `transcript_events` rows, about 240 MB in PostgreSQL. CLI built from this branch via `pnpm openclaw`. The same store was indexed three times with `openclaw memory index --agent main --force`:

| Build | Result |
| --- | --- |
| This branch | `Memory index updated (main): 1 file indexed.` exit 0 |
| `main` (`d902b29bc`): the 3 production files swapped back, rebuilt | `Memory index failed (main): Error [ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY]: Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory [task=sessionTranscript.session-entries admittedInputBytes=932 exchanges=0 stage=running]` exit 1 (the reported failure) |
| This branch again, rebuilt, same store after the failed run | `Memory index updated (main): 1 file indexed.` exit 0 |

After the successful runs, `memory_index_sources` holds `sessions/main/large-dm-session.jsonl` (251,257,868 bytes) and `memory_index_chunks` holds 90,000 rows.

**Focused tests:**
- `session-accessor.sqlite-read-hold.postgres.test.ts` against a live PostgreSQL 17.12 server, through `pnpm test` with the conformance preload: **3/3 pass**. With the 3 production files reverted to base, all 3 fail (one transaction and one unbounded head payload query instead of row-bounded slices). Running it live also corrected my original version of this test (second commit): two regexes and a slice count that couldn't have been checked without a server.
- `session-accessor.sqlite-read-hold.test.ts`, `session-memory-entry.worker.test.ts`, `session-accessor.sqlite-export-budget.test.ts` through `pnpm test`: **20/20 pass**. The initial revision also demonstrated that applying the 256-row cap to SQLite changed one transaction into three. The maintainer correction below restores its streaming behavior and pins it with a regression test.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`: clean. oxfmt and oxlint are clean on changed files.

### Maintainer verification on the additional reported workload

The original PostgreSQL fix is @Vaibhav2824’s. The follow-up limits SQL rows only on PostgreSQL. On identical isolated PostgreSQL 17 data, the shipped CLI indexed synthetic 360 MiB and 518 MiB sessions under the original 512 MiB worker limit. The larger session contained 56,825 events, including a 23 MiB tool result with eight synthetic image entries. Each session ended with a distinct retrieval marker.

| CLI build | Outcome | Elapsed | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Eager export (pre-fix) | Worker OOM, exit 1 | 14.70 s | 3,471,964 KiB |
| Contributor head `539d7753` | Indexed both sessions and returned both end markers | 16.21 s | 1,288,480 KiB |
| Corrected head `1768c0f6` | Indexed both sessions and returned both end markers | 13.23 s | 1,299,696 KiB |

The eager queries returned 39,450 and 56,825 rows. The corrected SQL admits at most 256 rows per query. On these inputs, any consecutive 256 rows contained at most 2,467,896 and 26,446,151 payload bytes respectively. A single oversized event can exceed the post-transfer 2 MiB decode threshold. The single paired run establishes recovery and RSS on this corpus. [Before/after run](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_402c7947e7a462216a3aff990df68f6b) · [Corrected CLI and regression tests](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_8935d8e922d082fb1102f37c05ea0ad2)

The corrected SQLite test failed on the preceding head with three transactions and passed with one. All 20 focused SQLite/worker tests and all three real PostgreSQL tests passed. The runtime build used for the measurements succeeded. A separate full build on `539d7753` exceeded the plugin SDK export declaration budget (5,406,367 bytes against 5,385,536). [Full-build run](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_d1fe3ba6fd99bce1a1af5b9071205f6e)

<details>
<summary>Local environment notes</summary>

Run on native Windows with Node 26.13. Two Windows-only tooling problems unrelated to this change came up and were worked around, not fixed: TypeScript 7's native compiler mishandles Windows extended-length paths when a checkout path is 248+ characters (so the run used a short-path worktree), and `scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs` passes a `C:` path to `--import` (so the same preload was supplied through `NODE_OPTIONS`). The `vector` extension wasn't available, so the e2e used keyword-only memory, which the docs support on PostgreSQL. The export path changed here is the same in both search modes.
</details>

prs.title: feat(signal): let a group reply to the bot count as a mention
prs.body:
Closes #161781.

## What Problem This Solves

Replying directly to OpenClaw’s message in a mention-gated Signal group leaves the follow-up unanswered unless the sender adds an explicit mention. Signal’s native Reply gesture is a common way to address someone in a group.

## User Impact

Quote-only replies stay quiet by default. Set `channels.signal.implicitMentions.quotedBot: true` for the `default` account or `channels.signal.accounts.<id>.implicitMentions.quotedBot: true` for a named account. With opt-in, an admitted sender’s quote counts as a mention when OpenClaw can verify that it sent the quoted message from that account in the same group. Quoting a human message from the same Signal account or an unmatched message still requires an explicit @mention. `channels.defaults.implicitMentions.quotedBot: false` disables quote activation for every Signal account.

## Why This Change Was Made

A human and OpenClaw can send from the same Signal identity. Successful OpenClaw group sends now mark the existing reply-context record keyed by account, group and Signal message ID. After sender admission, the adapter checks the quoted author and looks up that exact send before passing a quote-as-mention fact to the shared gate. Existing records still provide reply context. Quotes need an explicit @mention when the send marker is unavailable, including for pre-update records. This follows [Dan’s review guidance](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201148#issuecomment-7180622513).

## Evidence

### Verify the quoted OpenClaw send

- Commit `d1cc5f60a61eb3e433dad72058d47badcf0eb435` adds the same-account, same-group send check. Five new mention-gating cases dispatched unexpectedly on the prior quote logic. All 108 focused Signal tests passed on the revised tree in 77 seconds, covering actual outbound adapter registration with a stubbed Signal RPC transport, same-account human quotes, missing IDs, other groups and accounts, failed sends, and explicit mentions.
- All five reply-context worker tests passed in 73 seconds with local worker access. The new SQLite test reads an existing-format row, reloads the send marker after clearing memory, and verifies that ambiguous records cannot supply it. Signal type checking, targeted lint and formatting, MDX validation, generated config checks, and the import-cycle check passed.
- Hosted test timing is pending CI.

### Live exact-send and same-state upgrade proof (2026-11-26)

Live validation passed on `d1cc5f60` using Signal Desktop, an isolated Gateway, and a real model. With per-account opt-in enabled, a native quote of a verified OpenClaw send got a reply. Quotes of a direct Signal send from the same account and of a pre-upgrade bot message both reached the Gateway but produced no outbound reply or model turn for at least 54 seconds. An explicit mention on the direct-send quote still worked.

I upgraded the same saved state from OpenClaw and Signal v2026.11.10. The existing settings, selected model, session, and inbound/outbound reply-context records were retained. The new build continued the same session, persisted provenance for its own send, and successfully sent a native reply using the pre-upgrade reply context.

### Prior-head local evidence

- On the previous PR head `4cc1a65f`, four regression cases dispatched a turn unexpectedly. The cases cover the unset default, a shared default set to `true`, an explicit shared disable, and isolation between Signal accounts.
- On `33342fa7aa357640fbfebad9b76835a964bffb2f`, all 64 tests passed across the Signal mention-gating, account-resolution, and schema suites in 49 seconds wall time. They exercise synthetic signal-cli events through the production handler and verify which events dispatch a turn.
- Signal type checking, targeted lint and formatting, MDX validation, base and bundled config schema checks, config documentation baselines, and the import-cycle check passed. Hosted CI is pending. The live validation below covers the earlier account opt-in policy.

### Conflict refresh — 2026-11-24

Merged upstream `9a39176f4d7ea6808df5fc8f891306142e571df6` and regenerated the three conflicting config metadata and baseline files from the merged source. That refresh used head `409c40970fe1db070bc77bb2cc72d38bc06acdb4`.

All 93 focused tests passed in 79 seconds wall time across Signal mention gating, inbound context, account resolution, and config schema. Signal type checking, formatting, MDX, config schema and metadata checks, and the import-cycle check passed.

### Live Signal upgrade and opt-in proof

Validated on November 24 against the published `v2026.11.7` Gateway and Signal plugin, then against the built PR head `409c40970fe1db070bc77bb2cc72d38bc06acdb4` using the same isolated Gateway state. All inputs were sent from Signal Desktop to a private two-member Signal group. Native quote metadata was verified at the Signal relay. Positive cases ran a real model, had recorded output tokens, and were observed in the same group.

**Upgrade and data:** The candidate opened the saved stable state and kept the Signal channel configuration, group admission settings, and selected model. Startup refreshed metadata and added plugin and skill defaults. The stable reply was retained under the same persisted session, and the candidate’s explicit-address reply extended that session.

**Account controls:** Two logical Signal accounts used independent Gateway account streams backed by one registered Signal identity. A is the default account. B is the named test account. The first candidate phase used the stable config with no opt-in. The opt-in phase set the shared flag to `true` and opted in only B. The final phase kept B opted in and set the shared flag to `false`.

```text
stable A QR7BASEOK | explicit address | reply accepted and displayed, +9.6s, output_tokens=8
stable A QR7BASEQUIET | native quote | quiet 25s, outbound_attempts=0, transcript_rows=unchanged
upgrade A QR7UPQUIET | native quote | quiet 25s, outbound_attempts=0, transcript_rows=unchanged
upgrade A QR7UPMENTION | explicit address | reply accepted and displayed, +5.0s, output_tokens=9
opt-in B QR7OPTIN | native quote | reply accepted and displayed, +4.4s, output_tokens=8
opt-in A QR7OTHERQUIET | native quote | quiet 25s, outbound_attempts=0, transcript_rows=unchanged
shared-disable B QR7VETOQUIET | native quote | quiet 25s, outbound_attempts=0, transcript_rows=unchanged
shared-disable B QR7VETOMENTION | explicit address | reply accepted and displayed, +5.2s, output_tokens=10
```

Four replies and four quiet controls were verified. A send that lacked a relay receipt was retried and is excluded from the eight measured inputs. The isolated Gateway and relay were stopped after verification.

### Prior-head live Signal and stable-upgrade proof

The live test below ran on `4cc1a65fa2da8d6cc52c668dbcd94fb1e15a1abb`, before the policy change to account-scoped opt-in.

Used Signal Desktop in a private two-member test group, an isolated Gateway, and a real OpenAI API model. Started with the published OpenClaw and Signal plugin v2026.11.5, then switched the Gateway and plugin to the earlier candidate on the same test state. The group allowlist, `requireMention`, recent-history limit, and explicit `quotedBot: false` were preserved and checked. After testing the explicit opt-out, removed only that override in the test configuration to exercise the default.

```text
Stable v2026.11.5: explicit mention replied; quote-only stayed silent.
Candidate after upgrade, quotedBot=false: quote-only stayed silent; explicit mention replied.
Candidate with default policy: ordinary message stayed silent; quote-only replied.
Totals: 6 real Signal inputs, 3 expected same-group replies, 3 quiet controls.
OpenAI assistant turns with recorded output tokens: 3 of 3 delivered replies.
```

The live ingress receipts confirmed that the three quote inputs targeted the configured Signal account and contained no explicit mention. The positive quote reply was also observed in Signal Desktop.

prs.title: fix: stop large MCP tool catalogs from stalling the Gateway when a session starts
prs.body:
Closes #199327

Supersedes #199346. This PR carries @lonexreb's two commits from that PR unchanged, with their authorship. It adds the real-model Gateway proof ClawSweeper asked for there, which has been the only open item since November 15. The code is identical to #199346's reviewed head `f992f15609f`, applied to current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

Every new session that uses an MCP server with a large tool catalog compiles an output-schema validator for every tool on that server, on the Gateway's main thread, before the agent does anything. Sessions almost never call more than a few of those tools. On a production Gateway with a roughly 200-tool MCP server, this showed up as a main-thread stall of about 1.1 s each time a scheduled job or chat started a session, which delays every other channel and reply on that Gateway. The compiled validators also stay in memory for the session runtime's whole lifetime.

## User Impact

Sessions that load large MCP catalogs start faster, stop freezing the Gateway while they load, and hold much less memory. Output validation is unchanged: a valid structured result passes, an invalid one is rejected, and a tool whose schema references another tool's `$id` still validates on its first call.

One behavior differs. If one tool's output schema cannot compile, today the whole server fails to start and every tool on it is unavailable. With this change only that tool fails, when it is called. The rest of the server keeps working.

## Why This Change Was Made

See #199346 for the design. `normalizeMcpToolCatalog` keeps each included tool's output schema and compiles its validator on the tool's first call, then reuses it. Schemas that declare `$id` still compile at catalog load, in catalog order, so other tools' `$ref`s to them resolve no matter which tool runs first. Validators are not shared across session runtimes; that larger change stays out of scope, as triage suggested.

## Evidence

All runs were on this branch's head and on `main` at `0fa34123b32`, built with `pnpm build`, Node v26.13.1, Linux arm64.

### Real model, isolated Gateway

Setup: `node openclaw.mjs gateway run` with its own `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, `HOME` and port. The model was `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` with `agentRuntime: { id: "openclaw" }`. A synthetic stdio MCP server, `proof`, was registered with `openclaw mcp add`. It lists 204 tools, each with an `outputSchema`:

- 200 `bulk_*` tools with draft 2020-12 schemas of realistic size: nested objects, `$defs` and `$ref`s, enums, formats and patterns.
- `good` and `bad` share the schema `{ ok: boolean }`. `good` returns `{ ok: true }`, and `bad` returns `{ ok: "not-a-boolean" }`.
- `base` declares `$id: https://example.test/base`. `derived` is `{ type: "object", $ref: "https://example.test/base" }`.

The server never validates its own output, so only OpenClaw can reject a result. Each prompt ran through `openclaw agent --agent main --session-key <fresh key>`, so every turn started a new session runtime. The prompt was "Call the MCP tool `<name>` on the `proof` server once … reply with exactly the text of the tool result".

MCP server log on this branch, showing what reached the server:

```
03:23:35.289Z initialize
03:23:35.303Z tools/list -> 204 tools
03:23:38.405Z tools/call derived -> {"ok":true}
03:23:42.686Z tools/list -> 204 tools
03:23:45.937Z tools/call good -> {"ok":true}
03:23:49.859Z tools/list -> 204 tools
03:23:53.873Z tools/call bad -> {"ok":"not-a-boolean"}
```

Tool results the Gateway gave the model, from `openclaw sessions export-trajectory`, with the external-content wrapper trimmed:

```
derived (first tool called in its session) -> structuredContent: {"ok":true}
good                                       -> structuredContent: {"ok":true}
bad                                        -> Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: /ok must be boolean
```

The model's final replies were `{"ok":true}` for `derived` and `good`. `main` gives the same three results.

Usage per turn, read from the agent's result metadata: input 142, cache read 16,868, cache write about 17,400, output 132–312 tokens. Each turn is the opening request of a fresh session, so the cold cache is expected.

### Per-session catalog cost

This uses the built `normalizeMcpToolCatalog` and `createMcpJsonSchemaValidator` from each build's `dist`. It ran on the same 204-tool `tools/list` response and normalized it 25 times with a fresh validator provider each time, as each new session runtime does. Run with `node --expose-gc`, repeated 3 times; all three runs agreed to within 0.1 MB.

| | `main` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| First catalog load | 142 ms | 22 ms |
| Later loads (median, max) | 52.5 ms, 87–111 ms | 11.6 ms, 16–18 ms |
| Retained heap per catalog | 8.31 MB | 1.27 MB |
| Invalid structured output | rejected | rejected |

This work runs synchronously on the Gateway's main thread. Schemas in real servers can be much larger than this fixture's; the production stall above was about 1.1 s per session.

### Tests

- `pnpm test src/agents/mcp-tool-metadata.test.ts`: 17/17 pass on this branch.
- The same test file against `main`'s implementation fails "compiles an output schema on its first call only, never at catalog load (#199327)".
- `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` and `git diff --check` are clean on the changed files.

### Related, not changed here

The same runs turned up three things on `main` that this PR does not change:

1. A `$ref` to another tool's `$id` from a schema that declares `$schema: https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema` takes the TypeBox path and fails to compile with `unresolved ref`. On `main`, that one schema stops the whole server from starting ("MCP server proof unavailable"). On this branch only that tool fails, when it is called.
2. A tool whose output schema is a bare `{ "$ref": … }` with no top-level `"type": "object"` rejects valid results with "data must have required property 'result'". This happens on both builds.
3. With the Codex harness (`agentHarnessId: codex`), Codex calls MCP tools over its own connection, so OpenClaw's output validation is not on that path. The Gateway still loads and compiles the full catalog for each Codex session. That compile cost is exactly what this PR removes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

prs.title: fix: release generated model rows after a hosted catalog expires
prs.body:
Related to [#205737](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/205737), whose snapshot-retention failure was fixed on main by [#205761](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205761).

## What Problem This Solves

A long-lived model catalog worker can keep the declarations generated from a hosted publication after that publication expires. The registration configuration remains live and its manifest-row cache still holds the generated array.

## User Impact

The worker can release old generated declarations while continuing to reuse rows for the current hosted catalog. The change requires no configuration update.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing cache now holds the hosted publication weakly. This follow-up ties the generated rows to the same publication lifetime. The metadata snapshot still identifies manifest-only rows, and replacement planning must succeed before the cache changes.

## Evidence

- On main after [#205761](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1e7216ff679b5c689c0fa71015126846dc29c00a), the hosted publication collected. Its generated array and its individual model remained reachable on both Node 24.22.1 and pinned Bun 1.4.4. The test held the configuration and metadata through collection and made no intervening cache lookup. The synthetic projection had one row (177 bytes serialized as JSON).
- At `38a531b6`, both objects collected. Keeping the publication alive preserved the identity of its cached array and model across collection. All 28 tests in the model-catalog suite passed on each runtime, including publication, replacement, withdrawal, and planning failure. [Focused Linux x64 Testbox dispatch](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45762500243)
- The only change after that run renamed a bound test callback parameter to satisfy the repository’s shadowing rule. Pinned oxlint 1.89.0 checked both changed files with that rule enabled and returned zero errors. [Correction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ce7bcafb6ace7b4b7a8ef83e7e56c228d2fc7b6e)
- The diagnostic measured object reachability. The byte count describes the fixture's serialized content. Process memory and Gateway peak RSS were outside this comparison.

prs.title: fix(cli): refresh profile shims after Git release conversion
prs.body:
Closes #204146

## What Problem This Solves

After a checkout-to-Git-release conversion, the Gateway can start through the resident launcher while an existing managed profile's terminal CLI still runs the checkout. Terminal integration compares the release link path with the physical package path and skips replacing the old shim.

## User Impact

The profile's terminal command follows the selected release and keeps the profile default and Node runtime arguments. Other profiles keep their selected commands.

## Why This Change Was Made

When the verified service command names the profile's managed Git release launcher, validate the physical package entrypoint and keep the resident launcher in the terminal shim. This reuses the release selector for subsequent updates and retains the existing path for ordinary package and standalone installs. A named file without a release launcher header is left alone.

## Evidence

Verified on Apple silicon macOS with Node 26.12.1. A dedicated named profile, separate temporary config and a loopback Gateway isolated this check from the existing installations. I installed the latest stable build through the real Gateway CLI. From an external terminal I then installed the candidate by invoking the actual Git release launcher from the selected release slot with `gateway install --force`.

| Runtime check | Latest stable checkout | Candidate Git release |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profile shim `--version` | OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (`712ae03`) | OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (`b05be57`) |
| Resident launcher `--version` | — | OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (`b05be57`) |
| Authenticated `gateway status --deep --require-rpc --json` | RPC available, build `712ae0338512` | RPC available, build `b05be5771daf` |

The rewritten profile shim names the resident launcher. The installer reported that the pre-existing default selection was retained. The temporary LaunchAgent was unloaded and its plist and probe profile were removed from the account. This exercises service installation and reconciliation against real builds. The release artifact and link were staged locally for this check.

- The regression fails on `69ce03a30b`, where the executed shim still returns the original checkout output. It passes on `b05be5771d` with the real updater-generated launcher, filesystem links and fixture package entrypoints. It also verifies the next release selection, profile defaults, Node flags, an unrecognized launcher file and preservation of another profile's shim.
- 25 installer-definition tests, 10 resident launcher tests and 56 terminal/service-layout tests passed. One pre-existing login-zsh test selects the host CLI first and fails with the same output on the untouched base. Two tests were skipped by the runner.
- Core typecheck, targeted lint/format, and `git diff --check` passed. Runtime builds completed for both commits and emitted existing Control UI budget warnings on both. Hosted CI is pending.

An independent review of the local change identified the need to distinguish a generated launcher from a different file at the same path. The final patch checks the existing launcher headers and the regression verifies the unrecognized-file case.

### Native shim and subsequent release selection

On the installed candidate service, the generated profile shim kept the dedicated named profile and the service's actual Node argument `--max-old-space-size=8192`. Its command points to the resident Git release launcher. After the authenticated Gateway check and after unloading the test service, I atomically redirected the actual release link to a second built release and ran the same installed shell shim and launcher. Neither command required a shim rewrite.

```text
shim before link switch=OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (b05be57)
shim after link switch=OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (712ae03)
resident launcher after link switch=OpenClaw 2026.11.7 (712ae03)
shim bytes unchanged=true
```

This subsequent selection check exercises real CLI commands with built artifacts. The staged second slot uses the stable build as a distinct identity. The hosted CI workflow is awaiting maintainer approval. [CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45238543800)

Thanks to Hannes Rudolph for the release conversion trace.

prs.title: feat(models): split sign out on this device from disconnect account
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A saved OAuth sign-in in **Settings → Models** has one action: **Sign out**. It deletes the saved credential on this Gateway, but the grant stays active at the provider. A person who wants to remove OpenClaw's access to their account must find the provider's account page on their own, and nothing in Settings tells them that signing out and disconnecting are different.

## What Changed

**Plugin SDK (optional fields on the OAuth `ProviderAuthMethod`):**

- `revoke({ profileId, credential, config, signal })`: revoke this sign-in's grant at the provider. Resolve when the grant is revoked or already invalid; throw an `Error` with a user-facing message when it may still be active.
- `disconnectLabel` (default **Disconnect account**), `accountManagementUrl` (HTTPS only) and `accountManagementLabel` (default **Manage connected apps**).

**Gateway (existing owner `models-auth-status.ts`, no new method):**

- `models.authStatus` adds `oauthAccountActions` to providers with a saved OAuth/token sign-in, read from the loaded plugin registry. A status read never loads a plugin.
- `models.authLogout` accepts `revoke: true` with exactly one `profileIds` entry. The Gateway calls the plugin's `revoke` (30 s abort signal) and deletes the saved profile only after it resolves. If it throws, the profile is kept and the request fails with `UNAVAILABLE`: `<provider message> The sign-in is still saved on this device.`
- `ModelsAuthLogoutParamsSchema` gains the optional `revoke: true` field. Additive, no protocol version change; no stored-row change. The `models.auth*` schemas move unchanged from `agents-models-skills.ts` (at its 700-line cap) to a sibling `schema/models-auth.ts`; the protocol registry owner count goes from 76 to 77.

**Control UI (Models → Providers account row):**

- When the provider declares account actions, the OAuth account shows text actions: **Sign out on this device** (the existing sign-out), the plugin's disconnect label, and the manage link. Other providers keep the existing sign-out icon.
- Disconnect confirmation says that the provider revokes access and other devices that use this sign-in stop working, and points to **Sign out on this device** for a local-only removal.
- Failure: a persistent error toast `Couldn’t disconnect <account>` with the provider's message and **Try again**. The account stays in the list.

## User Impact

- Providers that implement `revoke` get a real disconnect; a refused revoke never shows as disconnected.
- Providers without these fields look and work as before.

## Evidence

**Gateway boundary tests** (`models-auth-status.test.ts`, 53 pass; protocol schema test accepts `revoke: true` and rejects `revoke: false`): status advertises the plugin's actions; revoke runs before removal (order recorded); a failed revoke keeps the profile and returns the provider message.

**Control UI E2E on a real Gateway** (`model-provider-disconnect.real-gateway.e2e.test.ts`, dist-nodts build of this head): a synthetic `acme` provider plugin loaded through `plugins.load.paths`, a seeded `user@example.com` OAuth profile and a local revoke endpoint. Light and dark: the row shows both actions and the link; with the endpoint returning 503 the toast shows the error and **Try again**, and the profile stays saved on disk. After the endpoint returns 200, **Try again** removes the account from the UI and from the persisted store. Every revoke request was `POST`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `token=<refresh>`.

Screenshots (before = base `427900b2d539`, after = this branch; synthetic `acme` plugin, `user@example.com`): see the images attached below.

**Disconnect retry scope:** `model-providers-page.removal.test.ts` › retries a refused disconnect only for the agent that asked for it (red without the scope check, green with it; found by local review round 1).

**Other checks:** touched UI unit suites (`profiles-view`, `view.provider-actions`, `data`, `model-providers-page.removal`, `model-providers-page.order`, `view`): 110 pass.

## Defaults recorded

- A failed revoke keeps the saved sign-in. Deleting it anyway would make the UI imply the account is disconnected while the grant may still be active. The person can still use **Sign out on this device**, or the provider's account page link.
- `revoke` takes one profile per request. Revoking several and removing only some would need a partial result shape; the UI never needs it.
- Account actions come from the plugin registry the Gateway has already loaded. A provider plugin that is not loaded (for example, a provider whose models run only through a core API config) shows today's sign-out until it is loaded.
- Disconnect (with its label) comes from the provider's first auth method that declares `revoke`; the manage link (with its label) comes from the first method with an HTTPS `accountManagementUrl`. They may be different methods (local review round 2).
- The core default labels are localizable; plugin labels are shown as given.
- `control-ui-performance` budget: `largest CSS gzip 57.3 KiB > 56.9 KiB` and the chat boot JS budgets fail identically on the merge base `427900b2d539` (same 58,659 B shared-styles file); this PR does not change that file.

prs.title: fix(lmstudio): report the context of a failed embedding preload
prs.body:
Related to https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/198830.

## What Problem This Solves

When LM Studio rejects an embedding model load, OpenClaw still gives just-in-time inference a chance. If inference also fails, the memory CLI reports “Model is unloaded” and drops the context length the loader tried. On a small host this hides the setting the operator needs to inspect.

## User Impact

The error now includes the context requested for the failed native load, after applying the model's advertised limit. It preserves the inference status, model and batch size. A successful inference still returns its vectors. This patch changes diagnostics only. The [sizing experiments](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/198830#issuecomment-7182498996) and [contributor troubleshooting PR](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199552) remain separate.

## Why This Change Was Made

The native loader knows the attempted context even when no instance is loaded. It now records that number independently of the existing chat decision to require a larger instance. The embedding adapter carries the failure through the individual request. Concurrent calls retain their own diagnostics and the embedding cache keeps its canonical model identity.

## Evidence

- Frozen main `9ad935f281e018f9c6941dc1bf20fddc809d1a83` failed the new loopback HTTP regression. Preload requested 32,768 and received 503. The subsequent inference returned 400. Main reported `Model is unloaded`. The patch also reports `preload requested 32768 context tokens`.
- The same controlled responses through the released 2026.11.3 CLI and the built candidate gave exit 1 in the double-failure cell. In the recovery cell the fixture forwarded inference to real LM Studio on Linux CPU. Each CLI indexed **8/8 files**, returned the expected top search result and completed nine successful embedding requests.
- An additional cold recovery started with zero loaded instances, rejected native preload, and finished with one real LM Studio instance and eight indexed files. During recovery two inference responses returned 500 and eight returned 200.
- Full package build, scoped lint, formatting and the documentation MDX check passed. Five focused provider, loader and chat-instance test files passed **63/63**. After correcting the existing chat cooldown fixture for the new constructor, the extension test typecheck passed and the complete LM Studio test selection passed **206/206** across 18 files on the [signed head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1ef2fc8e44c9027f7698c7d4fa3a668b0126dc46). The change adds 18 net production lines to retain the native fact and preserve the existing fallback decision, 44 net test lines and two documentation lines.

prs.title: fix: let your mid-turn messages reach CLI agents in resumed turns
prs.body:
Related: #202510

## What Problem This Solves

A message you send while a CLI agent (Claude CLI and other CLI runtimes) is in a turn started through the agent command path, such as the turn that resumes after `sessions_yield`, never joins that turn: the join is refused although nothing changed, so the message waits and gets its own later reply.

## User Impact

If you may steer such a turn, your message now reaches it mid-turn, as it already does for embedded turns and plain CLI DM turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

Joining a running turn checks that the message comes from the person the turn runs for, then compares the turn's recorded execution selection with the message's. For these CLI turns both checks read a wrong value:

- `agentDir`: the shared command builder (`buildCommonCommandRunParams`) left it out, so CLI runs recorded none. The builder now carries it for both runtimes (the embedded call's own copy is removed).
- `cwd`: the CLI capture recorded the cwd the runner had already derived; it now records the caller's cwd, as the reply and embedded producers do.
- Requester: CLI preparation binds the requester to the reply operation, not the placeholder attempt (#178865 moved the CLI requester projections there). The injection target's `requesterPrincipalKey` still read the attempt, got undefined, and every continuation fell back to a whole-policy compare that differs by design (`tool_authority_mismatch`). It now reads the operation for CLI runs, like the projections beside it. The added condition picks the right source; it skips no check.

The checks themselves are unchanged: a different person, cwd or agent dir still refuses.

## Evidence

**Live, before and after** (Telegram DM to a test gateway, claude-cli). The owner asks for a helper (`sleep 15`), `sessions_yield`, then `sleep 40` and a DONE line; 48 s in, during that `sleep 40`, the owner DMs "also include the word PELICAN<time> in your DONE line".

| Build | Resumed turn after `sessions_yield` | Plain DM turn (control) |
|---|---|---|
| `main@664bb5f1253` | refused (`tool_authority_mismatch`): the turn replies `DONE` at 74 s, then a separate turn replies `DONE PELICAN233514` | joined |
| this PR (`b6b087e0b86`) | joined: one reply at 82 s ends `DONE PELICAN234115`, no refusal logged | joined |

Either part alone is still refused, so both are needed. Tested on `b6b087e0b86` (on `main@664bb5f1253`; later main commits touch none of these files).

- Review: `autoreview` on `664bb5f1253..b6b087e0b86`, P0–P2: patch is correct, no findings.
- Tests (fail without the fix, pass with it):
  - `execute-plugin.steering.test.ts` (24.3 s): a running CLI turn in the agent-command shape; the requester's continuation is prepared, another person's is not.
  - `tool-authority.test.ts` (13.9 s): the CLI capture's selection equals an incoming reply's; a different cwd or agent dir stays unequal.
  - `attempt-run-params.test.ts` (11.1 s): the builder hands the agent dir to both runtimes.
  - Times are `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1` wall. `src/agents/cli-runner/`, `src/agents/harness/`, `src/sessions/` pass except `session-diff-revisions.test.ts`, which fails identically on plain main here (sandbox git setup). CI: awaiting workflow approval.
- **No request proof:** steering changes which turn receives a message, not any model request.

<details>
<summary>Claude Opus 5.5</summary>

Alternatives considered: for the requester, teaching the continuation join an exception for CLI targets would leave every other reader of the target's requester key wrong (it also feeds the collaborative-steering checks); the target producer is the one owner. For the selection, comparing effective values inside the gate would touch the shared check and is wrong for ACP-placed sessions, whose cwd is node-owned. An earlier revision defaulted `agentDir` inside the CLI capture by repeating the runner's own `resolveAgentDir` call; carrying the command's value removes that second derivation, which could drift from the runner's. The CLI runner already received `agentDir` from its other callers (automations, isolated completions, compaction), and the value the command path passes is the same `resolveAgentDir(cfg, sessionAgentId)` the runner would otherwise compute, so no runner behavior changes beyond the recorded selection.

</details>

prs.title: fix: say which agent's session store blocked an update and why
prs.body:
Related: #205202

## What Problem This Solves

When `openclaw update` (or `openclaw doctor --fix`) stops because Doctor cannot read a session store during the legacy-main session migration, the report ends at the redacted path and says nothing else:

```
Failing check plugin-doctor-post-session-state (blocked-by-session-repair-failure): Post-session plugin repair was blocked because prerequisite session repair failed: Error: cannot read legacy session store [redacted-path]
```

The operator cannot tell which store failed or why, so there is nothing to act on before retrying the update.

## User Impact

The same refusal now names the agent whose store failed and the cause, and the store path stays redacted:

```
Failing check plugin-doctor-post-session-state (blocked-by-session-repair-failure): Prerequisite session repair failed: Error: cannot read legacy session store for agent ops: StartupMaintenanceRequiredError: OpenClaw agent database [redacted-path] uses schema version 21; stop active
```

No behavior change besides the message: Doctor still refuses on an unreadable active store, and the update still rolls back. The unredacted error keeps the full store path at its end for local logs.

Not covered here, which is why this is `Related` and not `Closes`: the cause of the reporter's own read failure is still unknown (this change is what would show it), unreadable stores are not skipped, and `doctor --lint` does not gain a finding for them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both doctor-fix throw sites in the legacy-main migration wrote the store path before the cause. Support redaction replaces a path together with everything after it, so the cause never reached the update report. They now follow the cause-before-location order that `formatSchemaMigrationFailure` already uses: agent and cause first, store path last.

The fact is also capped at 200 characters, and the receipt's wrapper sentence used 83 of them before the error started, which cut a longer cause such as the schema-version message above. The refusal code and check id already say that the post-session plugin repair was blocked, so the receipt message now leads with the failure.

Detect-mode warnings and outcomes are unchanged. The helper lives in the scan module because the migration module is at its line cap.

## Evidence

Reproduced through the real Doctor CLI (`pnpm openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes`) on Linux, Node 24.22.1, with an isolated `HOME`, state directory and config, one agent `ops`, and three unreadable-store shapes. Before is `main` at `69b81b5a063`; after is this branch at `3e134893ed4`. Exit code is 1 in every run.

| Store problem | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Configured store file is not a database | `cannot read legacy session store [redacted-path]` | `cannot read legacy session store for agent ops: Error [ERR_SQLITE_ERROR]: file is not a database; store [redacted-path]` |
| Configured store is at schema version 21 | `cannot read legacy session store [redacted-path]` | `cannot read legacy session store for agent ops: StartupMaintenanceRequiredError: OpenClaw agent database [redacted-path] uses schema version 21; stop active` |
| Retired `main` store path is a directory | `cannot inspect legacy session store [redacted-path]` | `cannot inspect legacy session store for agent main: Error: session store is not a regular file: [redacted-path]` |

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| ![before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shu-chen-dot-ca/shu-chen-dot-ca/3d7f8fd33a2cf0d7a72a7a3d75406f1b498f8a99/draft_daffcc/ev_939713.jpg) | ![after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shu-chen-dot-ca/shu-chen-dot-ca/3d7f8fd33a2cf0d7a72a7a3d75406f1b498f8a99/draft_daffcc/ev_266d9e.jpg) |

- New regression in `src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.sqlite.test.ts` runs the real migration against an unreadable store (not a database, and a dangling link) through the Doctor refusal receipt and `DoctorStateMigrationRefusalError`'s update facts. It asserts the agent and cause are in the public fact and that the store directory is not. Red on `69b81b5a063` (2 failed), green on this branch.
- `pnpm test src/config/sessions/legacy-main-session-migration.test.ts src/config/sessions/legacy-main-session-migration.retained.test.ts src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.sqlite.test.ts src/commands/doctor-session-transcripts.test.ts src/infra/state-migrations.schema-diagnostics.test.ts src/logging/diagnostic-support-redaction.test.ts src/flows/doctor-health.update.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed.
- `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1 pnpm check:changed`: core typecheck, all core test typecheck shards, lint and format of the changed files, the line-cap ratchet and the other gates passed. One gate failed, `changelog attributions`, on `CHANGELOG/2026.11.10.md:8130`, which this branch does not touch. The Knip dead-code scan was skipped because it exceeds its time limit on this host. `git diff --check` is clean.

Gaps: the packaged updater (`openclaw update --yes --json` from an npm global install) was not run; the proof above is the candidate Doctor step from source. Nothing was run on macOS. No local autoreview or ClawSweeper review was run; neither tool is installed on this host.

prs.title: feat: let plugins explain provider errors in chat
prs.body:
Related to #204403

## What Problem This Solves

Provider plugins can classify a failed request, but cannot supply the explanation shown to users. Chat falls back to generic advice even when a plugin recognizes the failure.

## User Impact

An opting-in plugin can show a safe explanation in the existing failure pill and details, including after fallback and reload. Only the failure that ends the run supplies that notice. Existing plugins and old notices keep their default behavior. This adds no action link or Google-specific implementation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing assistant formatter selects and redacts the copy. The common failure throw carries it separately from diagnostics and status inference, including at the overload cap. The settled notice owns `summaryAsTitle`; attempt metadata carries no provider notice. Workspace preparation keeps precedence over earlier provider errors.

The reply builder receives the already resolved failure summary and selects its text, recovery presentation and title flag together. The handler settles that result directly rather than replacing its text afterward. This preserves configured locale and time zone when there is no provider hook. Aggregate billing guidance keeps precedence over the last model’s rejection. No recovery policy or public hook signature changes.

## Evidence

### Billing precedence regression

I reproduced the no-hook billing-first/listed-model-last regression on `760e975` in both the existing mixed-failure suite and a real built Gateway/UI. The first request returned a billing error; the fallback was successfully listed for its credential, then rejected chat. Saved chat showed only the last model’s rejection.

One condition inside the reply builder restores the existing aggregate billing precedence. I expanded the existing mixed-failure test rather than adding another suite or helper. The new case fails on `760e975` and passes on `65f53f6`; the original rate-limit-then-billing case remains. This repair changes two files (+26/-19), with one production line changed and seven net test lines added. The handler, hook contract, locale/time-zone handling, title flag and checkout settlement are untouched.

I ran 75 focused tests (68.14 s including preparation), core/test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, diff checks and both production builds. The selected tests cover the mixed chain, French/Tokyo regression, provider replies and host auth/preflight recovery. I ran pr-simplify; no extra machinery was needed.

The real Gateway/UI regression also fails before and passes after reload on the final sources (40.71 s, 6.30 s test time). Both providers were called, and the successful model-list requests were observed. The fixture supplies synthetic HTTP responses and catalog discovery, with no `formatUserFacingError` hook. No Gateway or UI was mocked. Temporary capture instrumentation is not committed.

[CI is green](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45760919377) on `65f53f6e43e68ae78cebc8597ee7466d72ed876b`. All four new proof images were downloaded without authentication, matched byte-for-byte and verified in the PR. The PR stays unmerged with auto-merge off. The bound autoreview tool is unavailable. External platform delivery and the live Gemini plugin combination were not exercised.

The complete PR against main’s merge base is 22 files, +367/-207 (production +250/-187, tests +115/-20, docs +2).

### Clean comparison

**Before `760e975`, after reload**

![Before: the final model rejection hides the earlier billing problem](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb5ed63e-51c2-4d6e-89c4-1c9d46f4f2f9)

![After: aggregate billing guidance is preserved](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01ccd508-e8bd-4c6d-bdf0-7965c0bef9f8)

### Annotated comparison

**Before**

![Earlier billing failure is hidden by the last rejection](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce577b4c-05ba-4539-9575-c79bde9f0775)

**After**

![Billing guidance survives the later model rejection](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b6858882-bfb5-4111-9055-0017ba380dfb)

Real-build captures on 2026-11-26, light theme, 1280×900, identical synthetic inputs. The existing recovery action is unchanged.

### Retained proof for the generic hook and earlier repairs

On `760e975`, three real Gateway/UI cases passed: rejected-key recovery, the plugin explanation through fallback/reload, and no-hook French/Tokyo reset time. The locale regression is also rerun in the current focused suite. The Control UI had already respected the locale; the earlier defect was in the external reply path. [Locale clean capture](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/de33d2fa-f0b5-4352-84df-f1bf5adbac0d) · [Annotated locale capture](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/06f52fa0-8596-4901-a0e5-469f3901f969).

prs.title: fix: reduce idle Gateway memory during chat archival
prs.body:
Superseded by [the existing archival reader PR](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201959). Its production module matches this one apart from comments, and it already carries the safety tests and a measured performance hold. The independent ARM64 results and the remaining gate are [recorded on that PR](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201959#issuecomment-7184003347). This draft preserves the focused regression test and its proof.

Related: #181432

## What Problem This Solves

A Gateway with no conversations to archive wakes two transcript readers for its once-a-minute archive check. On the official Linux ARM64 2026.11.10 image, the second reader handled 13 target inventories in 13 minutes. Each call restarted its five-minute idle timer.

## User Impact

The Gateway can check for inactive chats with one fewer resident reader. It keeps the same archive schedule, retention settings and restore behavior. No operator action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session-store discovery already has a reader for selecting and validating databases. The change reuses that reader for the inventory between those steps. The same registry snapshot, physical database custody, revocation checks and error propagation surround the read. Requests for transcript contents still use the foreground history reader.

Default archival made this recurring on fresh installations. The pre-auth shared-state SQLite writer is a separate owner. Thanks to @shivadityasingh for the original report and @rainman74 for the status-only Synology case. Their SQLite timeouts and swap exhaustion remain open. [Default archival](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199899) · [Historical writer investigation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205053) · [Synology report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/181432#issuecomment-7066464268)

## Evidence

Five interleaved pairs on AWS ARM64 each ran two real maintenance passes against an empty store in a fresh process. Both variants used the same build of `9096fa781436fffb8bc26b1b55a01e0171abb006`. The baseline restored only the prior worker-selection argument behavior in the built module. Every process reported zero archived and zero externalized transcripts on both passes. Per pair, both variants sent four prepares and two inventories. [Accounting and measurements](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_7706884e729cf6c668adb001c2d4a1c0)

| Owner measurement | Baseline median / p95 | Candidate median / p95 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Distinct target readers | 2 / 2 | 1 / 1 |
| RSS after first check, MiB | 390.1 / 392.1 | 345.4 / 350.9 |
| First check, ms | 1660 / 1674 | 1413 / 1428 |
| Second check, ms | 6 / 15 | 6 / 15 |

The new regression test recorded one foreground inventory on the parent and zero on the candidate. All 27 focused tests passed, including real archive and restore, opt-out, source replacement and worker errors. Core typechecking, targeted formatting, lint and the ARM64 build passed. The exact built head served a real loopback Gateway status response. [Red](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_6d53a0518cc7bb2a5b59f822558dbf96) · [Green](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_078865a97083edd39fa0a8454ac72423) · [Static checks](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_98e472bd10b36f61f40218fc1d406458) · [Build](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_6b490e1b8b51474dd13756297aa44b56) · [Exact-head status](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_9cc760976095008b6493882acbbc6587)

The full-Gateway comparison uses fresh state, one successful status call and 15 minutes with the same listener on a four-core Graviton. Acceptance requires both inventory and preparation to reach the same reader, lower +14-minute listener RSS and a successful status response. The 2026.11.10 candidate overlays only the worker-selection argument on the official release. The measurements are recorded on the existing PR linked above. prs.title: fix: explain how to reopen an unavailable automation link
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Control UI opens a direct link to an automation and the Gateway temporarily can’t read it, the page shows the technical failure without telling the reader how to reopen the linked automation.

## User Impact

- Before (synthetic Gateway response): “Online store is unavailable”
- After: “Couldn’t open this automation. Reload this page to try again.”

Reloading the unchanged URL retries the exact automation read. Missing and denied links keep their existing feedback. Scheduling, writes, permissions, Gateway error responses, and list Retry are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The direct-link reader already knows which operation failed. This uses that existing context to map only the `UNAVAILABLE` read to a recovery sentence. It neither adds a retry mechanism nor implies that the automation is missing.

**Skill in practice:** Name the failed action in the reader’s words, give one next step that works in this surface, and don’t reuse a recovery step meant for a different request.

## Evidence

- On current main (`0d6d318d2514`), the test confirmed that reloading reopened the same URL, but the original error failed the new copy assertion. The patch passed all 10 connected Chromium loading tests, including a fresh read for the same ID after browser reload. The Gateway responses were synthetic; this does not test a live storage outage.
- 25 focused page tests passed, including missing and denied links. UI test type shards, the i18n check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- [Before and after screenshots (clean and annotated)](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205777#issuecomment-7183666942).

Co-authored-by: @vyctorbrzezowski

prs.title: fix(update): check finalizer requester once and verify interrupted recovery by RPC
prs.body:
## Problem
The adopted update finalizer can reload full requester policy inside the callback that guards each filesystem mutation. Recursive cleanup invokes the callback for each entry. This matches part of the reported stack in #205547 but does not establish the cause of the prolonged stall. Interrupted managed recovery could also settle on HTTP readiness without proving the health RPC.

## Change
- Check requester policy at first admission in an adopted finalizer. Keep native executor and local ownership checks live on every mutation. Explicit admission still reads fresh policy; other callers retain their existing checks.
- Require a successful authenticated health RPC and matching version/build identity before existing interrupted managed-service recovery records success. Preserve rollback, ownership, and data-risk guards. No schema, config, or dependency changes.

## Route and target line
Per the [bridge rules](src/cli/update-cli/AGENTS.md), this is legacy in-place update code. On `main`, `update.run` for an owned install goes through `src/update/` (release directories plus a launcher trial). An isolated cell updating a `main` candidate to a newer fixture served the new version from `~/.openclaw/git-install/releases/…` and never started a migrated finalizer. On `main`, the changes reach:
- **Candidate side of a shipped updater's first update:** requester policy checked once in the migrated-finalize worker. This is candidate code, so it also runs on the hop from stock 2026.11.8/2026.11.10.
- **Helper:** RPC-verified interrupted recovery. On `main` it runs only on legacy routes that have not moved, none of which is `update.run`. Users get it only through the 2026.11.11 line, where the release branch still uses this updater (no `src/update/` at `v2026.11.10` or on `release/2026.11.11`). **Target stable line: 2026.11.11.** No backport was made.
- **Hop from stock 2026.11.8/2026.11.10:** stock code bounds the worker only when an explicit timeout is given (`v2026.11.10:src/cli/update-cli/update-command-migrated.ts:286,340`), and stock writes the helper source. The candidate worker and Doctor run during this hop, but a worker-side timer cannot bound a stopped process. A self-abort after candidate start would also end in the same pending state shown below. This PR does not add a candidate-side guard for that hop.

## Evidence
- Requester-policy patch: the new recursive package-settlement test failed on the base. On the fix, settlement of a 32-file backup checks requester policy once, keeps more than 32 native owner checks, removes the backup, and preserves the new install. Explicit re-admission detects revocation.
- Interrupted managed-service fixtures: HTTP-only settlement failed on the base and passes with the fix. The daemon probe rejects matching HTTP identity when an authenticated health RPC is required.
- A default worker deadline was tried and has been removed (`b9adfb02781c`), following ClawSweeper's P1. Without an operator deadline, finalization stays unbounded, as on the base (d79393ea). A joined timeout ends in a pending recovery that leaves the Gateway stopped (see the cells below), so killing a slow but still-progressing finalizer would make things worse. CI on `6688230ca9da` was green; CI on the new head is pending.
- The earlier local `update-command-doctor-authority-callers` failure was not caused by this PR. That run reported `Source changed during compiled subprocess invocation` because files were edited mid-run. The file passes 22/22 at `d7ff04f51065` in a network-none container and passes in CI.
- Service cells ran in private rootless Podman with systemd PID 1, a systemd user unit, synthetic state (12 agents), and an authenticated `update.run` over a loopback registry. The backport cells used the build from before the revert. That build still had the default deadline, which is not involved in the SIGKILL cells. A cell counts as verified only with authenticated `health` RPC ok **and** a `gateway status --require-rpc` build ID matching the expected package.
  - **(a) Normal, `2026.11.8 → exact candidate`** (`d7ff04f51065`, labeled 2026.11.10, package sha256 `6be033c5…`): reached terminal `succeeded`/`finished` in 4m30s. Health RPC ok. Serving build `2026.11.10-d7ff04f51065-2026-11-26T02-14-52.032Z` matches the package. Verification: `settled: true`, `readyz: true`.
  - **Stock first hop with a stalled worker, `2026.11.8 → candidate`** (explicit `timeoutMs: 420000`, worker sent SIGSTOP): the stock deadline fired after about 322s and cancellation settled. The updater reported `update-activation-timeout` with `serviceRestartSafe: false`. The helper logged `recovery not attempted: updater explicitly rejected activation`. **The Gateway unit was left `inactive (dead)`**, and `health` returned ECONNREFUSED ten minutes later. The explicit `timeoutMs` workaround bounds the wait but does not bring a Gateway back.
  - **(c) Owner killed during a stalled finalization, on a `release/2026.11.11` + this PR build → newer fixture:** the worker was sent SIGSTOP and its waiting updater was sent SIGKILL 20s later. The helper logged `handoff failed: managed update command lease binding was lost`, then `failed to finalize update run`, and exited 1. It never reached interrupted recovery because the still-living worker held the delegated lease. **The Gateway was left stopped.**
  - **Operator workaround after both processes were killed:** the Gateway stayed `inactive` and the ledger stayed at `running`/`activating` for 15 minutes. Then `openclaw update repair --yes` exited with status `warning`, `coreUpdate: completed`, and started the service. The Gateway then served `2026.11.12-d7ff04f51065-main-next-fixture`, which matches the fixture package, with health RPC ok.

## Open proof and scope
This PR does **not** meet the requirement that a timed-out or interrupted finalizer ends with a verified successor or a verified restored predecessor. It does not close #205547.
- **Timeout:** any worker timeout, explicit or inherited, surfaces as `UpdateCommandPendingRecoveryFailure` (`update-command-unwind.ts`: owned handoff not completed) with `serviceRestartSafe: false`. The helper then leaves the Gateway stopped, as the stock explicit-timeout cell shows.
- **Killed owner:** once the updater has delegated the executor to the worker, killing the waiting updater makes the helper fail with `lease binding was lost` **before** it reaches `recoverInterruptedUpdater`. A second cell killed both the worker and the waiting updater (`release/2026.11.11` + this PR → newer fixture) and got the same result: the Gateway stayed `inactive`. So the RPC check added here is correct at fixture level but is not reached in either installed SIGKILL cell. The fixtures do not model the delegated lease. Until that is fixed, recovery takes a manual `openclaw update repair`.
- **What closing this needs:** a joined worker timeout and a dead delegated executor must both route into the existing verified interrupted-recovery owner. That changes the stopped-Gateway recovery policy and lease custody, so it needs maintainer agreement first.

## Reconciliation (2026-11-26)

- **Where this matters.** The helper-side and updater-side commits (`e193237d270d`, `8e47da50fb55` RPC-verified interrupted recovery; `b9adfb02781c` unbounded finalization) take effect only on a line whose own updater is this legacy code, which today is **2026.11.11**. They are carried and completed there by https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205758 (`fix(update)[2026.11.11]`). That PR routes an operator-timeout finalizer stop and a lost updater or worker into the verified interrupted recovery. Like `b9adfb02781c`, it keeps finalization bounded only by an explicit timeout (its head `e978dfa8e13e`). A hang inside the Doctor phase still ends in the existing data-at-risk stop; that is left open there for a maintainer decision.
- **main.** `update.run` goes through `src/update/`. Isolated cells on `origin/main` `1140fc54a32d` show that path already meets the #205547 bar without changes. A launcher trial SIGSTOPped before ready rolled back after its 20-min budget, and the previous build served, verified by authenticated health RPC and build ID. A launcher plus candidate SIGKILL during the trial ended with the new build verified serving. A Gateway SIGKILL during release preparation left the previous build serving within 18 s.
- **Recommendation.** Land on `main` only if maintainers want the candidate-side piece: the requester policy check once in the migrated-finalize worker, plus the `healthRpcVerified` probe field. That code runs when a shipped 2026.11.10/11.11 updater updates *to* a `main` release. Otherwise close this PR in favor of #205758. `b9adfb02781c` (no implicit deadline) is consistent with #205758 and can stay.

## Worked on by

- @RomneyDa

prs.title: feat: support host-managed sessions_spawn attachments
prs.body:
## Summary

- add a stable `sessions_spawn.attachmentRefs` handoff for host-managed multimodal attachments
- wire the admitted turn's staged-media handles into the shipped tool construction path
- reject nonempty reference lists on visible sessions, which do not support attachment staging
- resolve references only through a Gateway-owned authorization callback
- validate image MIME, configured size limits, exact byte count, and SHA-256 before staging
- preserve existing inline attachments and forward validated images to ACP
- add contract tests and documentation

## What Problem This Solves

Multimodal tools can produce native image content without a safe, update-resilient way to hand it to a spawned child. Inline base64 serialization is unnecessarily large and makes authorization and provenance difficult to enforce.

This keeps bytes host-managed: the model supplies only a validated reference envelope, while the Gateway resolver controls whether the reference is current and authorized. The child receives the same private staged attachment path used by existing attachments.

## Evidence

- `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.attachments.test.ts` covers an authorized reference and stale/unauthorized failure.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-spawn-tool.schema.test.ts` covers the public `attachmentRefs` schema.
- `git diff --check` passes locally.
- The implementation reuses existing private staging, sandbox projection, configured byte limits, and SHA-256 receipt generation.
- `createStagedMediaAttachmentResolver` now resolves only handles from the admitted turn's `stagedMediaPaths` map; unknown handles fail closed.
- Visible sessions reject nonempty `attachmentRefs` before session creation.
- Added production-resolver and visible-spawn rejection tests.

## Testing

- Added coverage for authorized references and stale/unauthorized failure.
- Added schema coverage for `attachmentRefs`.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- Full test suite not run locally because this checkout does not have dependencies installed.

## Review remediation (9c96dd085)

- Generated image results now issue short-lived, session-bound `attachmentRef` envelopes containing the host-computed byte count and SHA-256; the model receives the envelope in the result text/details and can pass it to `sessions_spawn`.
- Staged relative paths are resolved against the admitted sandbox/workspace root before the host media boundary is consulted; arbitrary paths remain unavailable.
- Resolver MIME is derived from the file bytes with the image signature detector. Spoofed image MIME metadata and non-image bytes fail closed.
- Added resolver coverage for workspace-relative paths and MIME spoof rejection.
- Focused Vitest execution remains blocked locally because `pnpm` and `node_modules` are unavailable in this sparse checkout.
