issues.title: Feishu: broadcast-only @all wakes the bot and produces a spurious reply
issues.body:
## Problem

In Feishu group chats, a **broadcast-only `@所有人` mention** (`@_all`) is treated as a mention of every bot in the group. With `group_policy: "mention"`, the bot therefore wakes up on announcements it was never addressed in, and emits a spurious reply.

Root cause is one line in `nanobot/channels/feishu/runtime.py`:

```python
def _is_bot_mentioned(self, message: Any) -> bool:
    raw_content = message.content or ""
    if "@_all" in raw_content:
        return True
```

Feishu delivers `@_all` inside `content`, and there is no check against `mentions`, so `True` is returned before any `open_id` comparison happens.

There is an upstream test named `test_at_all_always_matches`, so this looks intentional rather than an oversight — hence this issue proposes an **opt-in** switch instead of changing the default.

## Why "just reply with nothing" does not work

Returning an empty final answer does not produce silence: `nanobot/agent/loop.py::_persist_turn` replaces an empty `TurnKind.USER` response with `EMPTY_FINAL_RESPONSE_MESSAGE` ("I completed the tool steps but couldn't produce a final answer…"). So the model is forced to emit visible text, and the group sees noise either way. The filtering has to happen at the mention-detection layer.

## Reference implementation

OpenClaw handles this explicitly in `extensions/feishu/src/mention.ts`:

```ts
export function isFeishuBroadcastMention(mention): boolean { ... }
export function checkBotMentioned(msg, botOpenId): boolean {
  return msg.mentions.some((m) => !isFeishuBroadcastMention(m) && m.id?.open_id === botOpenId);
}
```

i.e. a broadcast-only `@all` / `@_all` never matches, and `docs/channels/feishu/access-control.md` documents that behavior.

## Proposed change

Add an opt-in config flag `ignore_mention_all` (alias `ignoreMentionAll`), default `false` so existing group behaviour is unchanged; when enabled, `@_all` alone no longer counts as a mention of this bot.

```python
    def _is_bot_mentioned(self, message: Any) -> bool:
        raw_content = message.content or ""
        if "@_all" in raw_content:
            if not getattr(self.config, "ignore_mention_all", False):
                return True
            # broadcast-only @all: fall through to the real mention check
```

`getattr` keeps it working with duck-typed config objects in tests.

Verified locally: `pytest nanobot/channels/feishu/tests/test_feishu_mention.py` — 8 passed (3 new cases: default keeps old behaviour, `@_all`-only is ignored when enabled, real `@bot` still matches when enabled).

## Patch

```diff
diff --git a/nanobot/channels/feishu/config.py b/nanobot/channels/feishu/config.py
index 2587c1694..7be7de9bf 100644
--- a/nanobot/channels/feishu/config.py
+++ b/nanobot/channels/feishu/config.py
@@ -19,10 +19,14 @@ class FeishuConfig(Base):
     allow_from: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
     react_emoji: str = "THUMBSUP"
     done_emoji: str | None = None
     tool_hint_prefix: str = "\U0001f527"
     group_policy: Literal["open", "mention"] = "mention"
+    # Feishu @所有人 (@_all) reaches every bot in a group. By default it counts as
+    # a mention of this bot (long-standing behaviour); set this to true to treat a
+    # broadcast-only @_all as NOT a mention, matching OpenClaw's semantics.
+    ignore_mention_all: bool = False
     reply_to_message: bool = False
     streaming: bool = True
     domain: Literal["feishu", "lark"] = "feishu"
     topic_isolation: bool = True
 
diff --git a/nanobot/channels/feishu/runtime.py b/nanobot/channels/feishu/runtime.py
index 083f82ab5..abebe468e 100644
--- a/nanobot/channels/feishu/runtime.py
+++ b/nanobot/channels/feishu/runtime.py
@@ -1286,11 +1286,14 @@ class FeishuChannel(BaseChannel):
 
         return text
 
     def _is_bot_mentioned(self, message: Any) -> bool:
         raw_content = message.content or ""
-        if "@_all" in raw_content:
+        # @_all is Feishu's "@everyone" placeholder. A group can ask for it to be
+        # ignored so broadcast-only messages never wake the bot; a message that
+        # also mentions the bot directly still matches via the loop below.
+        if "@_all" in raw_content and not getattr(self.config, "ignore_mention_all", False):
             return True
 
         for mention in cast(list[Any], getattr(message, "mentions", None) or []):
             if self._is_bot_mention_event(mention):
                 return True
diff --git a/nanobot/channels/feishu/tests/test_feishu_mention.py b/nanobot/channels/feishu/tests/test_feishu_mention.py
index dacb99550..f76fe03e1 100644
--- a/nanobot/channels/feishu/tests/test_feishu_mention.py
+++ b/nanobot/channels/feishu/tests/test_feishu_mention.py
@@ -1,17 +1,18 @@
 from types import SimpleNamespace
 
 from nanobot.channels.feishu.runtime import FeishuChannel
 
 
-def _make_channel(bot_open_id: str | None = None) -> FeishuChannel:
+def _make_channel(bot_open_id: str | None = None, ignore_mention_all: bool = False) -> FeishuChannel:
     config = SimpleNamespace(
         app_id="test_id",
         app_secret="test_secret",
         verification_token="",
         event_encrypt_key="",
         group_policy="mention",
+        ignore_mention_all=ignore_mention_all,
     )
     ch = FeishuChannel.__new__(FeishuChannel)
     ch.config = config
     ch._bot_open_id = bot_open_id
     return ch
@@ -40,10 +41,22 @@ class TestIsBotMentioned:
     def test_at_all_always_matches(self):
         ch = _make_channel(bot_open_id="ou_bot123")
         msg = _make_message(content="@_all hello")
         assert ch._is_bot_mentioned(msg) is True
 
+    def test_at_all_ignored_when_configured(self):
+        ch = _make_channel(bot_open_id="ou_bot123", ignore_mention_all=True)
+        msg = _make_message(content="@_all hello")
+        assert ch._is_bot_mentioned(msg) is False
+
+    def test_at_all_with_direct_mention_still_matches_when_ignored(self):
+        ch = _make_channel(bot_open_id="ou_bot123", ignore_mention_all=True)
+        msg = _make_message(
+            content="@_all hello", mentions=[_make_mention("ou_bot123")],
+        )
+        assert ch._is_bot_mentioned(msg) is True
+
     def test_fallback_heuristic_when_no_bot_open_id(self):
         ch = _make_channel(bot_open_id=None)
         msg = _make_message(mentions=[_make_mention("ou_some_bot", user_id=None)])
         assert ch._is_bot_mentioned(msg) is True
 
```

Happy to adjust naming, default, or drop it in favour of a different approach if maintainers prefer. Since PRs are currently limited to collaborators, posting this here first as the contributing guide asks — please let me know if you'd like an actual PR branch and I'll hand it over.

issues.title: WebUI: option to auto-convert long pasted text into a workspace file instead of inlining it in the message

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

issues.body:
### Problem / Motivation

When pasting long text (logs, articles, config files, command output) into the composer, the entire text is inlined into the chat message. This:

- pollutes the conversation transcript with a wall of text,
- bloats session history and context for content that is usually referenced once,
- is awkward to handle on mobile, where selecting/re-pasting long text is error-prone.

The TUI already shows large pastes as a compact placeholder in the composer, but the text is still sent inline and unchanged.


### Proposed Solution

An opt-in setting (e.g. **Settings → Composer → "Convert long pastes to file"**, with a configurable threshold like 2,000 characters) that, when a paste exceeds the threshold:

1. saves the pasted text to a file in the active workspace (e.g. `inbox/2026-11-25-paste-1.txt` or a configurable directory),
2. replaces the inline text in the message with a short reference (path + size + first line),
3. lets the agent read the file like any other workspace file.

Nice-to-haves:

- A per-send override (e.g. a composer toggle or "send inline anyway" button) for cases where the text must stay in the message.
- Same treatment for oversized tool results already exists ("saved files for oversized text tool results"), so this would make user input consistent with that behavior.


### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

Other

issues.title: Windows: native TUI fails to install Bun when a virus scanner locks bun.exe (WinError 32)
issues.body:
### Summary

On Windows, `nanobot agent` cannot start the native TUI on first use when an antivirus scanner is active. The pinned Bun runtime is downloaded and verified, but moving it into the cache fails with `WinError 32`, so the TUI is unavailable and only `--no-tui` works.

### Reproduction

1. Windows 11, antivirus active, no Bun 1.3.13 on `PATH` (a different global Bun version, e.g. 1.4.5, does not count because the version is pinned exactly).
2. Remove `~\.nanobot\tools\bun\1.3.13` if present.
3. Run `nanobot agent`.

```
Downloading Bun 1.3.13 (windows-x64-baseline)…
Native TUI unavailable: Could not prepare Bun 1.3.13: [WinError 32] The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process: ...
```

### Cause

`ensure_bun()` in `nanobot/bun.py` writes `bun.exe` into a `.install-*` temporary directory, runs `bun.exe --version` to verify it, and then immediately calls `os.replace()` to move it into place. A virus scanner inspects the freshly written and executed binary and briefly holds it open, so `os.replace()` fails with a sharing violation and there is no retry.

Side effects: the verified `bun.exe` stays behind in a `.install-*` directory, nothing is cached at the final path, and every following start downloads the ~117 MB archive again and usually fails the same way.

### Proposed fix

Retry the move for `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (`winerror == 32`) for a bounded time (e.g. every 0.5 s for up to 30 s) and re-raise all other errors immediately, so non-Windows behavior is unchanged.

A tested fix with a focused regression test in `tests/test_bun.py` is available here: https://github.com/NobseVomBerg/nanobot/tree/fix/bun-windows-locked-replace

I verified it manually on Windows 11 with an active scanner: the download completes, `bun.exe` lands in the cache, and the TUI starts.

prs.title: feat(webui): edit and resend messages in the same session
prs.body:
**Current head: `e8b8a1466`, based on `main` at `c360a10e8`.** [All 20 CI checks passed](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/45754519320), including `CI required`. **Not requesting review yet:** the fixed-main Windows comparison passed three of five latency gates.

A latest HTTP history page can arrive before two ordered WebSocket edit notices. The client now keeps the current reply in that case and revalidates notices across deletion/recreation of a chat key. Bounded one-chat model checks and actual client/SQLite probes cover these interleavings, exact receipt retries, stale sources, and late events. The checks assume atomic SQLite commits and FIFO socket notices; they are not an unbounded correctness proof.

Production gateway + Chromium checks on `6c87df802` passed desktop/mobile cancel with focus restoration, first/middle/paged resend (0/3/174 inputs retained, one model call each), two tabs, refresh and reconnect. Only model transport was a loopback fixture. The only subsequent change was to the app-layout **test fixture**; no production code changed.

Eight fresh Windows gateway pairs × 16 matched samples per operation (640 pairs total). Paired median Δ and one-sided 95% upper bound / margin, in ms; positive is slower:

| Operation | Median Δ | Upper / margin | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Latest history, 8 turns | −0.35 | +0.39 / 1.00 | Pass |
| Latest history, 192 turns | +0.07 | +1.18 / 1.00 | Not established |
| Ordinary input → ACK | −0.04 | +0.24 / 1.00 | Pass |
| Ordinary input → completed reply | +0.57 | +2.18 / 5.00 | Pass |
| Warm navigation → latest bubble + frame | +3.50 | +6.35 / 5.31 | Not established |

Long-read block median deltas ranged from −1.55 to +2.78 ms; render from −1.40 to +9.50 ms. These intervals do not establish a regression or meet the non-regression gates. No measurements pooled across heads. `main` has no equivalent edit operation. Earlier results below remain historical.

Related to [NAN-92](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92/webui-支持编辑并重新发送已发送的用户消息).

## What users get

In a saved topic, select **Edit message** beside your message on desktop, or under **Message actions** on mobile, to open an inline draft. **Cancel** preserves the conversation and composer. **Resend** replaces the selected message and its suffix and generates a reply in the same topic. **Fork** still makes a separate topic. This does not undo external tool effects. Edit the text of ordinary messages, including captions on uploads and local file attachments. Resending reuses the original files rather than uploading them again. If a file is missing or access has been revoked, the conversation and draft stay intact. Quotes, mentions, commands and special inputs are not converted to plain text. [User guide](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/a51f1ea21be4420ea50e9728bc64777db8d6bb49/docs/webui.md#edit-a-sent-message).

## Current behavior and verification

Edit-and-resend is an in-place fork at the selected input. A normal fork copies the prefix to a new topic; resend keeps that prefix in the same topic and writes the replacement. Both use the same prefix and transactional persistence code. A later append is not a conflict: resending at B discards an already appended C. A normal message sent after the replacement continues the current topic; it has no history-version precondition. A genuinely missing fork point cannot select a different row. Other connected tabs receive the replacement over WebSocket.

The session transaction stores the replacement and the original attachment references in the existing durable input queue. The worker then handles that input exactly as it handles a normal send. The model loop has no edit/fork branch, and a retry does not generate a second reply. Local file access is checked again before truncating the conversation.

On `25d2bcdbf`, two Chromium tabs on the production-built local gateway verified both message ordering and attachment reuse with a real model. A text file was uploaded once; changing the question made the model retrieve a different value from that same file. The second tab updated without reloading and the file remained attached after refresh. The restart regression also exercises resuming an accepted, not yet executed replacement with an image. Focused Python, UI and browser checks, the production build, type checks and import boundaries passed. Two unrelated startup-language UI tests also fail on the preceding head. The earlier Windows benchmarks were not rerun.

## Earlier verification (`68c11eaf0`)

[Earlier CI](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44917107465). Synced `main` at `0dc8679ed`. On desktop and a 390px viewport, opening the editor on a collapsed message exposes the full text and resend controls; cancel restores the original collapsed message and keyboard focus. Edit admission no longer decodes answer bodies to identify the discarded suffix. A concurrent SQLite writer test verifies that a history page and its ETag describe the same snapshot and an edit based on an obsolete page is rejected.

### Historical comparison: `0dc8679ed` vs `68c11eaf0`

Both snapshots were separately production-built on Windows and run against the same deterministic loopback model, fixture data, dependencies and browser. Eight fresh gateway pairs × 16 measured pairs per operation; startup and within-pair order were balanced. Differences are PR minus `main`, in ms. For all five shared operations the one-sided 95% upper bound on the paired median was below the existing margin. This measures typical latency on this runner, not every device or tail latency.

| Shared operation | Paired median Δ | One-sided 95% upper bound | Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Latest history (8 turns) | -0.29 | +0.61 | 1.00 |
| Latest history (192 turns) | -0.83 | +0.25 | 1.00 |
| Ordinary input acknowledgement | -0.20 | +0.20 | 1.00 |
| Ordinary input → completed reply | -2.44 | +0.56 | 5.00 |
| Navigate → latest message painted | +0.60 | +4.90 | 5.00 |

`main` has no edit-and-resend operation, so it has no like-for-like timing for that new feature. Earlier results against an older integration parent and the previous edit implementation are [historical diagnostics](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92#comment-59285eab-02f7-45da-bd22-d08700295c79), not the readiness gate. [Measurement plan, all 640 raw pairs and confidence intervals for the current comparison](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92#comment-03da91ef-d8e0-464f-940a-7719408576c5).

## Correctness evidence on `e42f74689`

- One owner serializes ordinary input and edits. The SQLite transaction checks the page-independent source identity, original text, revision and retry receipt, then changes both model history and display history. Admission failure leaves the old histories intact. Once accepted, a model failure belongs to the new turn. A transport retry does not schedule a second model request.
- **White-box:** reviewed admission/dispatch, cancellation, storage/crash boundaries, outbound ownership, HTTP pagination and frontend draft/connection lifecycle. Fixed canonical `input_id` on replacement and a late idle event that could leave its original run marked active. The late event releases only that owner and does not publish into a replaced history. Final focused Python selection: 81 passed.
- **Black-box:** two Chromium clients, production-built UI, real local gateway/SQLite/WebSocket and a deterministic HTTP model. Mouse, keyboard and touch; cancel with an outstanding composer draft; middle, first and paginated edits; reload and actual disconnect/reconnect. The provider saw exactly 3, 0 and 174 retained user inputs respectively, followed only by the edited input, once per edit. Older retained rows remained pageable; the topic/identity did not change. Two editors of the same revision produced one winner; reconnect/retry, busy/stale source, provider refusal and ordinary fork were checked independently. No uncaught browser exceptions. No physical device or external model was used.
- **Formal concurrency check:** [two TLA+ models, assumptions and reproduction commands](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/tree/e42f74689b0e41915d0c7d52939092cd50f4b062/verification/history-edit). All invariants held over 484 admission states and 132 delayed-delivery/reconnect states, with no unexpected deadlock. Removing transactional source validation or the retired-generation fence gave the expected counterexamples. These are bounded single-owner models assuming atomic SQLite commits, not an exactly-once guarantee for external side effects.

## Historical CI and snapshots (`e42f74689`)

[Test Suite 44722331397](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44722331397) passed, including `CI required`. PR head `e42f74689`; Actions checked out `5a0fd420d`, merging that head onto `db0306b40`. The local correctness and timing runs use the PR head; ordinary timing uses its frozen integration parent `cd75dbfaa`, not moving main. No check or size/coverage budget was relaxed. Attempt 1's Windows native upgrade/recovery test reached the second `metadata-loss` journey, then `inspect_profiles()` raised `ValueError` while checking readiness after the second restart. The exact target's push CI skipped native acceptance. The preceding PR candidate passed the same step. Only that Windows job and downstream aggregate were re-requested on the unchanged merge; the original failure is not attributed to the edit without evidence. [First attempt's failure report](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44722331397/artifacts/14624090600).

<details><summary>Historical performance results and diagnosis on e42f74689 (superseded by the current table above)</summary>

### Performance

**At that snapshot, performance was not signed off:** Latest page, 8 turns, Latest page, 192 turns, Ordinary input → completed reply, Navigate → latest message painted, Edit → completed reply. Do not treat passing CI as performance approval.

Windows, real same-version gateway/WebUI with a deterministic loopback model. Ordinary operations vs `cd75dbfaa` (integration parent); edits vs `d06d326ad` (previous edit implementation). Four fresh gateway pairs, 16 measured pairs each, per metric. Snapshots on the same volume. AB/BA balanced at startup and randomized within adjacent pairs; warmups excluded, no other observations discarded. Reads decode eight real HTTP responses per observation. Render requires the expected message in view followed by an animation frame. Edit replaces turn 49 of 96, with one provider execution and the exact retained prefix. All durations are ms.

| Path | Baseline median | PR median | Paired Δ [two-sided 95% interval] | One-sided upper / margin | Gate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Latest page, 8 turns | 13.21 | 14.36 | +0.88 [-0.28, +1.62] | +1.54 / 1.00 | Not established |
| Latest page, 192 turns | 14.70 | 15.27 | +0.64 [-0.51, +1.60] | +1.19 / 1.00 | Not established |

prs.title: fix(providers): keep parallel tool calls apart when the stream omits index
prs.body:
Gemini's OpenAI-compatible API streams parallel tool calls without `tool_calls[].index`: each call arrives whole (id, name and arguments) in its own chunk, and the turn ends with `finish_reason: "stop"`. `_parse_chunks` falls back to the call's position inside its chunk when `index` is missing. That's 0 for every one of these chunks, so all the calls of a turn land in one buffer: the id and name of the last call win, and the arguments are concatenated.

Replaying a captured `gemini-3.5-flash` stream with two parallel `get_weather` calls through the `openai` client and `_parse_chunks`:

```
before: call_4234487 get_weather '{"city":"Paris"}{"city":"Tokyo"}'
after:  call_4234484 get_weather {'city': 'Paris'}
        call_4234487 get_weather {'city': 'Tokyo'}
```

### Change

A delta without `index` now starts a new call when it carries an id different from the current call's id, or a name on an id-less call that already has one. Anything else is appended to the current call, so providers that stream unindexed argument fragments keep working. Deltas that do carry `index` are handled as before.

### Tests

- `test_parse_chunks_keeps_parallel_calls_without_index_apart`: the two-call Gemini shape from the capture (thought signature shortened). It fails on `main` and passes with the fix.
- `test_parse_chunks_appends_unindexed_fragments_to_the_last_call`: id-less argument fragments still join the current call.
- `tests/providers` plus `tests/agent/test_gemini_thought_signature.py`: 1464 passed.
- `ruff check nanobot/`: clean.

This change was made with Claude Code; the tests above were run on the branch to check it.

prs.title: fix(exec): separate foreground commands from background session capacity
prs.body:
Previously, even a short `git status` had to reserve a background session before it could start. A handful of live previews could block every new shell command.

This PR separates foreground execution (8 concurrent, queued) from the 32 background slots shared by chats and subagents in a gateway. A command only needs a background slot if it outlives its initial wait. At capacity, promotion waits for an ongoing stop if possible; otherwise it stops the oldest background process tree. Its owner can poll for `preempted_capacity`. Reading or stopping an existing session takes no new slot. No new tool parameters.

Scope: exec scheduling and the runtime wiring needed to share capacity while keeping process ownership separate. No changes to archiving, session storage, sidebar behavior or clients.

Verification: 54 focused tests passed locally on Windows, covering capacity, concurrent promotions, queued launches, owner isolation and child task cleanup.

Resolves [NAN-503](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-503)

prs.title: feat(settings): add removable provider connections
prs.body:
Provider connections currently reappear as empty defaults after configuration reload, so removing an entry cannot persist. Store only connections the user has added, expose removal in settings, and let the running gateway respond when its selected connection is removed or restored.

Depends on #6145. Merge the independent UI improvements first, then retarget this PR to `main`. The base branch `feat/webui-model-settings-ux` mirrors the UI PR head so this diff contains only the subsequent provider connection changes.

## Changes

- Keep absent built-in provider entries absent through load, save, and reload. Persist explicit empty OAuth connections as `{}` while retaining credentials in their existing token stores.
- Add the provider-removal settings operation and distinguish connection presence (`has_config`), setup readiness (`configured`), and OAuth authentication (`oauth_authenticated`).
- Connect the settings removal control and add-again flow to that contract. Removing an OAuth connection retains its sign-in while clearing connection-specific fields.
- Include connection presence in runtime cache identity. Removing the selected connection switches the gateway to an unconfigured runtime; adding it again rebuilds the client.
- Register connections after successful OAuth login and onboarding, and adapt provider consumers to absent entries.

## Upgrade blocker

This PR remains a draft until legacy OAuth configuration migration is handled. A Codex configuration saved by the base version can omit `providers.openaiCodex`; loading that file here rejects the selected model as unconfigured before consulting its independent credentials. A base-save/new-load probe reproduced this behavior, and adding an explicit empty entry restored routing. This change is excluded from #6145.

## Validation

- 1,167 tests passed across the affected configuration, CLI, provider, runtime, and WebUI API files.
- Ruff passed for the updated tests. Earlier Ruff and strict BasedPyright evidence applies to the unchanged provider implementation.
- Provider removal UI and its regression test are preserved from the original implementation. The earlier 420-test WebUI run covers that implementation; the independent UI keyboard fix is verified in #6145.

## Why

Opening a file diff could download the Markdown parser even when the conversation had no rendered Markdown. The packaged WebUI also shipped a second copy of Shiki's language and theme assets inside the diff worker, even though the worker receives the resolved grammar and theme from the page.

## What changed

- Specialize the production worker build for Pierre's worker context, so Rollup drops the unused language and theme loading paths.
- Give the shared HTML serializer its own chunk. The production build checks that the worker does not regain the Shiki catalogs and that syntax highlighting does not pull in the Markdown vendor chunk, even indirectly.

## Scope

Initial app loading, language support, and Vite's chunk warning limit are unchanged. Large-chunk advisories remain; the goal is to remove unnecessary work, not clear the warnings.

## Blast Radius

The change affects emitted browser and worker assets only. Both the normal Markdown renderer and the worker-backed diff renderer still need the shared serializer or the resolved grammar as appropriate. No gateway, protocol, or persistence changes.

- Mark their WebUI replies as side-channel messages in both live delivery and history. Give the delayed Dream result its own WebUI identity so it can arrive after the command's `turn_end` without inheriting that turn's sequence or replacing a new answer.

## Verification

- Reproduced the metadata loss and the interrupted WebUI answer in regression tests before the fix.
- 48 focused Python tests and 274 WebUI tests passed, including a Dream result delivered and replayed after `turn_end`. WebUI build, typecheck, targeted lint and import boundary checks passed.
- Slack and Telegram route metadata is covered by automated regressions; no live workspace or bot was used.

prs.title: fix: verify downloaded Bun at its final cache path
prs.body:
Closes #6784.

A first source launch on Windows can fail if a scanner keeps the staged `bun.exe` open after its version probe: installation still needs to rename the file at that point. Move the checksum-verified executable atomically into the cache before running `bun --version`, and keep the install lock through validation. Remove an unrunnable download instead of returning it. The pinned version and system Bun reuse are unchanged.

This avoids renaming a file after executing it. It does not add retries for files already locked before the rename.

Verified on Windows with a real read handle held open from the version check onward and a fixture archive: the regression test failed with WinError 32 before the change and passed afterward. All six tests in `tests/test_bun.py` passed locally.

issues.body:
### Bug Description

When the gateway process that runs a turn is killed while a `terminal` command is in flight (we SIGKILL the largest process in the container, as the OOM killer would pick it), the owner-death supervisor correctly stops the command. But on `hermes chat -r latest -q "Continue."` the history no longer contains the call or a result for it: the assistant turn reads only "Running it.\nThis turn did not complete. Some actions may already have run; verify their effects before resending." The orphan-recovery path that keeps a dangling side-effecting call with an UNKNOWN result (`strip_dangling_tool_call_tail` in `agent/replay_cleanup.py`) is not what the resumed session shows.

With real models this matters. In a session where the command had already written its effect, five open model families (DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, MiMo V2.6 Flash, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Qwen3.8 Flash; 3 runs each) ran the command again in 11 of 15 resumes, six of them after reading the file and seeing the effect. When the same history kept the call with Hermes's own Ctrl-C result ("[Orphan recovery: interrupted side-effecting tool may have executed; its effect is UNKNOWN. Inspect state before retrying.]"), they repeated it 2 times in 15. Rewriting only the text (call still erased, the UNKNOWN wording naming the command) gave 8 in 15, so keeping the call is what helps. Where the command had been stopped before it took effect, every model ran it exactly once under the kept call's UNKNOWN result (15 of 15), so that result does not make models skip work that never happened.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `hermes chat --yolo --oneshot -q "Append two lines to build.log …"` with a model whose first `terminal` call is `echo one $(date +%s.%N) >> build.log; sleep 30`.
2. While the command sleeps, `kill -9` the `hermes_cli.main … gateway run` process.
3. `hermes chat -r latest --oneshot -q "Continue."` and look at the request sent to the model.

### Expected Behavior

The resumed history keeps the call with an UNKNOWN-effect result, as the dangling-call recovery does ("this tool may have executed before Hermes stopped; its effect is UNKNOWN. Inspect current state before retrying."), so the model knows which action may have run.

### Actual Behavior

The call and its result are gone; only the notice remains in the assistant turn (3 of 3 runs, model-free). A model that follows the task runs the command again.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory); CLI (interactive chat)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

`hermes debug share --local`, in the container the runs used (agent.log omitted: plugin registration lines only):

```shell
--- hermes dump ---
version:          unknown [(unknown)]
os:               Linux 6.8.0-117-generic aarch64
python:           3.14.9
openai_sdk:       2.54.0
profile:          default
hermes_home:      ~/.hermes
model:            scripted
provider:         custom
terminal:         local

api_keys:         (28 providers listed, all "not set"; the endpoint is given with --provider custom --base-url)

features:
  toolsets:           hermes-cli
  mcp_servers:        0
  memory_provider:    built-in
  gateway:            stopped (docker (foreground))
  platforms:          none
  cron_jobs:          0
  skills:             0
--- end dump ---
```

### Operating System

Debian 12 (bookworm) container, Linux 6.8 aarch64

### Python Version

3.14.9

### Hermes Version

v0.23.3 (tag, commit caafe538, installed from its source with the uv.lock, so `hermes --version` prints `vunknown (2026.9.24)`)

issues.body:
# RFC: THE DOC-CHAIN SUBSTRATE'S NETWORK — the read, the governance, the compaction


---

## The theme

The durable record survives the session's compression with its provenance intact, and the agent re-reads it rather than make the user repeat — the read restored, the store re-readable, the compaction governed, as one network.

## So what?

A Hermes user should be able to say "you're not listening" and have the agent re-read the durable record rather than make them repeat — and the record they anchor should survive the session's compression with its provenance intact. The doc-chain's network is the shape that gets there: the bounded read (Finn763's PR), the memory store's restore (#141876), the governed compaction (the provenance-origin + the K-recency, staged for their own home).

## The background

The read action's removal (56ee8a5cc6, 2026-02-19 — the 14-line removal) bought the compensation: 106 commits and 6,275 lines of undifferentiated heavy lifting on the memory path. The record counts 106 commits and 6,275 lines on the memory path [V — 56ee8a5cc6..HEAD, tools/memory_tool.py + tools/memory_tool_store.py: 106 commits, 6,275 lines = 3,541 added + 2,734 deleted], but the debt is a SUBSET, not that total. The subset is the code that exists only to hand entries back because the store cannot be read — four sites in tools/memory_tool_store.py, ~30 lines in all: _failure_with_entries (:322, over-budget consolidation carrying the live entries), the closest_entries hint (:124, the no-match error echoing the three nearest entries), the replaced-entry fields (:481 removed_entry, :488 replaced_entry — the batch op echoing what it touched), and the batch-abort's echo-fix (_batch_failure, :328-:336, carrying closest_entries so a retry does not re-echo the whole inventory). That subset is the one that pays for the restore: give the agent MemoryStore.read (the 12-line method #141876 puts at :369) and these echoes are the obvious first cut. The remaining thousands are the dreaming prototype, the soft-compression path, the doc-chain substrate — real work that STACKS on the symptom rather than closing it (root-cause leg 3). Count the subset, not the total. [A on "first cut / pays for the restore": #141876 as scoped does NOT delete these four sites — whether each then deletes or stays as defensive UX is the dive the owning work must do, not a claim to land in the body.] 

...and the tracked "class" still open — ten tickets that are really TWO classes, split by root, not by the memory label:

- SEVEN the RFC acknowledges SEPARATELY (the silently-dropped-value class, NOT the read):
  #99957, #105243, #49195, #105248, #140935 are the hermes -z oneshot class — the
  one-shot path drops a configured value or flag (max_turns, --resume) and never passes
  it on; #110126 and #50132 are the same shape on the config/compression path
  (max_output_tokens, compression max_tokens dropped before the wire). None is caused by
  the read removal; each has its own fix in flight (#61152/#99994/#105248/#140980 for the
  -z class, #128990/#106571 for the output-cap class, #50139 for the compression cap).
  The RFC names them, credits them, and points at their owners — it does not claim them.

- THREE the RFC KEEPS (the memory content-lifecycle class): #116673 (the bounded read —
  MEMORY.md anchors a doc chain — the one active proposal piece), and its two neighbors
  #135039 (write-time budget + acceptance pipeline) and #69264 (the memory-hygiene
  curation skill) — the content lifecycle of the store the read serves. The restore's the reversal already on the table (#141876, c0wb0yp0tat0, head `af16e3ab16`); the bounded read's Finn763's open PR (#116673); the governed compaction's a separate issue, staged but not opened.

## The current condition

The read action's removal caused a compensation toil the total overstates: ~30 lines of
  it are the four hand-entries-back sites above; the rest is adjacent work that stacks on the
  symptom (root-cause leg 3). The read path crashes on the PR head, is cleanly removed on the substrate, and works only in the experimental state — the three-state spread, each cell a run on disk:

- **The PR head** (#139606, `5b31ccb7d5`) — the read-action battery can't load; the cell's a collection error, not a clean 0/35.
- **The substrate** — `MemoryStore.read` cleanly absent; the read-action battery RED, 23 failed where the read's missing.
- **The experimental** — the uncommitted 14 lines + the untracked battery wire the read end-to-end; 35/35 green.

**Independent confirmation (jfugalde, 10-24):** on current main the tool answers `Unknown action 'read'`; on #141876's head, the entries plus the usage line, first try — the gap confirmed by a reviewer's execution, not just the RFC's own runs.

The K-recency window improves exact-recitation at every compression ratio on the 150-cycle sweep (2×–32×, K=10: +1.1/+2.2/+1.1/+2.3/+2.2pp), +2.2/+1.1/+2.3pp at the headline 4×/8×/16×. The honest scope of that number: the pipeline's real compressor ratios, the paraphrase step mocked, pruning off, the probe's own K=0 baseline (not the paper's 20.4/15.6/15.1). The long-session reverses it — 300 cycles, K=10 lands 6.1% against the 9.6% baseline, −3.5pp.

The stress battery (every cell cross-checked to a named artifact): 200/200 write-then-read, 800/800 concurrency survivors (0 corrupt, store not wiped), 100/100 re-read idempotence (content stable, done-flag steady), 20/20 over-budget refusals (graceful, entries preserved not wiped). The compaction-boundary gate holds: a non-user write to a protected scope's refused (Stage 2.c), the over-budget reroute-to-chain-doc seam returns `None`.

## The call-out

Stated plainly, then left for the room.

The sessions this substrate runs aren't the 150-cycle probe's — they're the real ones. The work's spanned over a month: the day's final run passed 22+ hours, the documented figure a ~799× session extension over a bare context window. The night arcs fire near midnight, with the first check-in at ~04:30; the runs last as long as the need dictates.

And the doc-chain substrate held through all of it — the anchor the pointer, the chain the unbounded layer, the reload-on-compression discipline keeping the run grounded turn after turn. That's the field record: sessions this long, this productive, the durable record surviving the compressions a bare-window run wouldn't. It's the proof-in-practice's cousin to the falsifier battery's lab proof — the lab says the mechanism's right; the marathons say it already works, in the wild, on the ambient team's era.

This is the statement awaiting the peer review's moment. The two reactions it's offered: "yeah, so what" — a long session's just a long session; or "wow, that's amazing" — a small, read-less, compaction-governed substrate carrying multi-hour, multi-turn productive runs a bare window can't. The call's the room's.

The nuance, held honestly: the *why* behind it — the compaction fidelity, the provenance, the field's convergence (LOHA/ACD's recitation floor, SJC's 83%) — rides here from the web storm's findings as the storm's source, NOT vetted truth in this RFC. What needs the verification goes through the enrichment process with the teams, not asserted into this call-out. The session lengths themselves're the rig's documented record; the interpretation's the storm's, pending.

## The root-cause

The 5-whys, the legs the record holds:

1. **The symptom** — the 6,275 lines of compensation churn (the churn's defensible core is the
  ~30-line subset above; the total is the stack, not the cause). *Cause:* every session must re-derive what a single read gives, because the read's absent.
2. **Why absent** — the read action was removed (56ee8a5cc6), not deprecated; the substrate carries no `MemoryStore.read`.
3. **Why the churn persists** — the compensations (the doc-chain substrate, the dreaming prototype, the soft-compression path) each answer the read's symptom, none its root; they stack rather than close.
4. **Why the compaction loses fidelity** — at the lossy cut-point, two things die that the anchor's non-lossy boundary never had to carry: the exact recent text (paths, shas, args — the K-recency reason) and the identifier back to a unit's origin (the provenance reason).

The verified legs: 1–3 (the churn, the removal, the stack-not-close) — the record's. Leg 4's two sub-causes each map to one measured field failure — the exact-text loss to LOHA/ACD's recitation floor (2609.31430), the provenance loss to Source-Judged Compaction's 83% (2610.20927). **The unverified leg (flagged, not asserted):** *why the read crashes on the PR head specifically* — the record shows the collection error, not its parent bug; that's the dive-deep the owning PR must still do. **Now verified by execution (10-24/25):** the collection error was the stale base, not a read bug — jfugalde's run and Finn763's rebase of #116673 (head `ffc651bd11`, clean, mergeable) closed it; both on the record, reported here, not re-derived.

## The target state + the gap

**The target** — the read restored on the substrate (the #141876 reversal, green where it's RED today); the durable record's provenance surviving a compression with its origin resolvable; the K-recency window holding its measured gain (or improving) at every ratio *and* not reversing in the long session.

**The gap** — today the read's absent on the substrate and the compaction's ungoverned. The gap's exactly the proposal's pieces: the restore's unmerged (#141876 open), the bounded read's unmerged (#116673 open), the compaction governance un-built. No numeric target's been signed off — the acceptance criteria below're proposed from the battery, the team's to confirm.

## The scope

- **In** — the bounded read (#116673); the read action's restore (#141876); the three in-scope complements (the reference-as-provenance framing, the recency-ordered read, the scroll-up's re-read); the governed compaction (the provenance-origin classification, the archive-before-stub, the K-recency hard window).
- **Out** — the reroute-to-chain-doc seam's *placement* (an open question, not a scope line yet — the two-way door below); any write-path or non-doc-chain memory work; the lossy-layer compaction itself, which belongs to the separate issue, NOT to #116673 (that PR never compresses or rewrites a body). *The out-of-scope line's a candidate for the team's confirmation, not an asserted boundary.*

## Why this RFC, why now

The comments on the two threads just went live with the honest test data and the first-timer's caveat — because the designers in the room should see what the connections enable before any of it gets decided piecemeal. This is the discussion's formalization: the network shown whole, the veterans' coaching welcomed, the mechanisms judged by the evidence on the record. And the field's reading the same terrain — the ecosystem's radar names memory governance the next competitive battleground, both projects moving from "memory storage" to "memory governance" (trust, budget, audit, access pipeline), the middleware window opening (big_model_radar's report). The discussion's timely, and the evidence's on the record.

## The proposal

The network, each piece in its home — and the connections between them, the way the threads framed it: the bounded read is the anchor the whole thing hangs from; the restore is the retrieval the listening mechanism rides on; the dreaming prototype (the quiet-hours consolidation, the session preservation cycle) and the compression work (the K-recency and provenance on the compaction path) live in their own homes, never stretching the anchor's scope; and the scroll-up's re-read is the read action's second life — a correction triggers a re-read, not a request to scroll up and dig it out, the agent scrolling up itself instead of asking twice. One network, each piece in its place, the connections load-bearing.

1. **The bounded read** (#116673 — owner: Finn763) — the chain-doc reference + the read/patch semantics, as scoped.
2. **The read action's restore** (#141876 — owner: c0wb0yp0tat0) — the retrieval the listening mechanism rides on; the 14-line reversal of 56ee8a5cc6.
3. **The three in-scope complements** — the reference-as-provenance framing, the recency-ordered read, the scroll-up's re-read.
4. **The governed compaction** (the separate issue — relates to #116564, the parent gap) — the provenance-origin classification, the archive-before-stub, the K-recency hard window.

**The landing order (jfugalde's sequencing, adopted):** #141876 first — 16 lines, additive — then re-cut the bounded read (#116673) on top of the restored read rather than beside it.

## The acceptance criteria

Proposed from the battery on disk; the team's to sign off the thresholds:

- [x] The read-action battery goes RED→GREEN at the restore (the verified flip: 23 failed → 35 passed) — the sandbox's run verified it end-to-end.
- [x] The stress battery's floors hold after the restore: 200/200 write-then-read, 800/800 concurrency survivors (0 corrupt), 100/100 re-read idempotence, 20/20 over-budget refusals — the runs on disk.
- [ ] The K-recency window's falsifier: it measurably improves exact-recitation at the 4×/8×/16× headline ratios (the +2.2/+1.1/+2.3pp held) — the gain's on the runs.
- [ ] The long-session hard gate — PASS/FAIL, not an open question. At 300+ agent cycles the K-recency window's exact-recitation must sit ≥ 0pp vs the K=0 baseline — never below — measured at the compression ratios production sessions actually run (4×–8×), evaluated across the whole run, not at the headline ratio alone. Any single measured point in the 300+ band below baseline at any ratio in 4×–8× fails the gate. This is the field's bar (3oltan-seo): a multi-hour production contour does not ship on a short-session extrapolation.
  - Status today: FAIL. The current data does not clear it — 300-cycle, K=10 landed 6.1% vs the 9.6% baseline (−3.5pp), below the line. The 150-cycle falsifier passing is necessary but not sufficient.
  - The honest caveat — the ruler's broken, the gate's not waived. The −3.5pp isn't the final word, and it isn't grounds to waive the gate. Across the runs the 300-cycle delta was non-reproducible (−9.2 to +10.2pp), root tracing to a scope bug in the probe itself — the measurement, not the window, was confounded. Under mock-forced paraphrase the window held stable at +1.1pp. So today's result is a broken ruler, not a reading: it can't certify the window safe, nor broken. Both the −3.5pp headline and the +1.1pp mock-stable are disqualified as certifying evidence until the probe's fixed. The gate stands — the Governance Decay reproduction (recency eviction → 100% violation, arXiv 2606.22528, DeepSeek-V4) is exactly the tail a soft gate lets through.
  - Measurement protocol: (1) fix the probe's scope bug first, no certifying run on the old probe; (2) sweep to and past 300 cycles to the field's longest contour, fixed K=10; (3) report per-cycle/per-bin Δ at every ratio in 4×–8× plus the headline ratios — the whole curve, not the endpoint; (4) baseline named and fixed; (5) paraphrase real, not mocked, for the certifying run (mock +1.1pp is a sanity check only); (6) judged on the worst case, not the mean — pass only if minimum Δ over all cycles ≥300 is ≥0pp at every 4×–8× ratio; one sub-zero point = FAIL.
- [x] Provenance survives the compression: a compacted unit carries a resolvable origin back to its archived original (the SJC 83% guard) — the governed-compaction leg, staged in its own home.

## The open questions

- Does the K-recency window scale with the session length? (The long-session reversal's a real finding: −3.5pp at 300 turns — the window must scale.)
- Should the caller's provenance default to "unknown" at the pipeline's definition, not just the call site?
- Where does the reroute-to-chain-doc seam land — this pipeline's follow-up or the governed compaction's home?

## The invited reviewers

The people I'm grateful for — the ones who engaged with me on GitHub as I'm new to the surface and have learned so much from every single interaction. This is a thank you, and a come-join-the-talk: the door's open to the room, and the invitations themselves go in the opening comment when this posts, where the @-mentions notify. This section is the record:

- @Finn763 — the bounded read's author ([#116673](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/116673)), the thread's owner
- @uni5592427 — the acceptance pipeline's author ([#135039](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/135039))
- @jimy-r · @RemanenetSpy — the thread's designers
- @alt-glitch · @teknium1 — the engaged, the field's voices
- @whyyagswhy — the restore's verifier, the RFC's referrer
- @xngg1021 — the one-shot bug work's helper, the classes' checks, the early-on confirmation that I was on the right track — a special thank you
- @binhnt92 — the early gut instinct of calling it out, the thread's first nudge — a special thank you
- @binhnt92 · @George-RD · @Enough1122 · @area51tazz · @xlionjuan · @3oltan-seo · @icegs · @GottZ · @liuhao1024 · @kvnloo · @jfugalde — the direct network's members and engagers
- @ZacharyThomasStone · @Im4EverDead — the trust circle

The invitation's the general engagement's — never the VIP treatment, never the exclusion — the door's open to the room.

## The two-way doors

Each decision's stated reversible with the available data; the direction's the room's:

1. **The K-recency window's size-and-scaling** — reversible (a window's a parameter; scale it with the session or fix it and re-measure). The −3.5pp@300-turn finding makes this the live one.
2. **The provenance default = "unknown" at the pipeline definition** — reversible (a default's a line change).
3. **The reroute-to-chain-doc seam's placement** — reversible (follow-up vs. compaction home; the open question above).
4. **The three complements' framing** (reference-as-provenance, recency-ordered read, scroll-up re-read) — reversible with the available data.

**The one-way door, flagged so it's not missed:** the archive-before-stub's *archive* side's cheap to reverse (the original's on disk); the *stub* side, once a working copy's replaced, leans on the archive's resolvability. Keep the archive-before the stub, always — that ordering's the only part that isn't freely reversible.

## The ownership

- The bounded read (#116673) — **Finn763**.
- The read action's restore (#141876) — **c0wb0yp0tat0**.
- The governed compaction (the separate issue, relates #116564) — staged in the pivot draft; the issue's to be opened by its author.

## The follow-up

The enrichment process with the teams follows the discussion's decision. The verification leg: the RED→GREEN re-run on the substrate, the stress battery's re-tally post-restore, the K-recency falsifier at the signed-off ratios, the long-session scaling probe, the provenance-survival end-to-end on the compaction issue.

## The no-blame note

This is a review of the system's state, not the actors'. The removal was a decision made in good faith (56ee8a5cc6, @teknium1); the 6,275 lines of compensation were the class's best effort at a root the decision didn't name. The design's elegance deserves the naming: the read's absence at the memory-store level, the fewer hops, the streamlined system — the 14 lines that would have been the amplifier it was designed to be. And the same class, done by hand on a single machine — a headless workstation that peaked during the Obama administration — the teams and the silicon that made it happen — the same amplifier, the same gift. issues.title: caller-side `a2a_call` times out at 420s regardless of `a2a_agents.<peer>.timeout` — concurrent tool batch deadline (`_DEFAULT_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S = 420`) clips every long A2A peer call

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: comp/plugins
labels.description: Plugin system and bundled plugins

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
Companion to [janpuc/home-ops#1372](https://github.com/janpuc/home-ops/issues/1372).

## Symptom

On the **caller** side (`hermes-main`), every `a2a_call` to a configured peer (`hermes-aether`) returns "agent did not reply in time" after **exactly 420s** of wall-clock, regardless of what `a2a_agents.<peer>.timeout` is set to in the caller's `config.yaml` (verified with `timeout: 3900` — the rendered config is correct, the live pod is on a post-merge ReplicaSet, no env-var shadow). The receiver (`hermes-aether`) is correctly set with `A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT=3600` and answers cleanly within that window when called directly via `curl message/send` (verified: a 450 s sleep on aether returns in 461 s wall-clock, HTTP 200, body has `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`).

So the A2A wire is fine; the 420s ceiling is upstream of the wire.

## Root cause (verified)

`agent/tool_executor.py` line 110:

```python
# Generous: slow-but-valid tool work must never be preempted by the batch guard.
_DEFAULT_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S = 420.0
```

When the caller model picks `a2a_call` from the concurrent tool batch (the normal path on hermes-main), `execute_tool_calls_concurrent` (line ~1423) resolves `timeout_s = _resolve_concurrent_tool_timeout()` with this 420s default. After 420s the worker is abandoned, the underlying `urllib.request.urlopen(..., timeout=3900)` keeps running as an orphan, the tool returns the failure text, and the main model's turn resumes.

For the sequential path, line 783 exempts `delegate_task`:

```python
_SEQUENTIAL_DEADLINE_EXEMPT_TOOLS = frozenset({"delegate_task"})
```

— but `a2a_call` is **not** in the exempt set, even though it carries the same orphan-batch hazard (the same comment on lines 779-782 calls this out explicitly: "under the 420 s deadline every real batch 'timed out' while its children ran on as orphans"). And the concurrent path (line 1423) has **no** exempt set at all, so every concurrent `a2a_call` is clipped.

## Evidence

- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 110: `_DEFAULT_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S = 420.0`
- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 168: `default=_DEFAULT_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S` of `_resolve_concurrent_tool_timeout`
- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 774: `return resolve_timeout("tools.sequential_call", default=_resolve_concurrent_tool_timeout())`
- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 783: `_SEQUENTIAL_DEADLINE_EXEMPT_TOOLS = frozenset({"delegate_task"})`
- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 832: `timeout_s = None if function_name in _SEQUENTIAL_DEADLINE_EXEMPT_TOOLS else _resolve_sequential_tool_timeout()`
- `agent/tool_executor.py` line 1423: `timeout_s = _resolve_concurrent_tool_timeout()` (no exempt check)

The configured peer timeout (`a2a_agents.<peer>.timeout`) flows to `urllib.request.urlopen(..., timeout=...)` in `plugins/platforms/a2a/tools.py:57` and is **correctly** 3900 for hermes-aether — so the urllib call honors 3900 — but it gets abandoned before that by the batch timeout. So the peer-level timeout knob is effectively dead for any concurrent a2a_call longer than 420s.

## Repro

Caller (`hermes-main`):
1. Pod `hermes-main-798fd77587-pr8d7` started today after `home-ops` PR #1361 merged (configmap shows `a2a_agents.hermes-aether.timeout: 3900`).
2. Main loop picks `a2a_call(agent="hermes-aether", message="sleep 500; date")` — the call lands in the concurrent tool batch.
3. After ~420s the tool returns an error string; the main loop continues.
4. Meanwhile the orphan urllib call on the worker thread may still complete and write to the context, but the model already moved on.

Receiver (`hermes-aether`):
1. Same `sleep 500` via `curl -m 600 message/send` from inside the `hermes-main` pod returns HTTP 200, `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, in ~310s for a 300s sleep and ~461s for a 450s sleep. So the wire is fine; only the caller-side batch wrapper clips.

## Proposed fix (locus, not patch)

Both upstream, in `agent/tool_executor.py`:

1. **Exempt `a2a_call`** from the sequential deadline (alongside `delegate_task`):

   ```python
   _SEQUENTIAL_DEADLINE_EXEMPT_TOOLS = frozenset({"delegate_task", "a2a_call"})
   ```

   `a2a_call` already self-bounds via `peer.timeout` (urllib); the wrapper should not double-bind it.

2. **Make `execute_tool_calls_concurrent` honor per-tool exemption** (introduce `_CONCURRENT_DEADLINE_EXEMPT_TOOLS` or a per-tool override mechanism), so a concurrent `a2a_call` is not abandoned by the 420s batch ceiling.

3. **Or**, expose the existing override knobs more visibly:
   - `timeouts.tools.concurrent_batch` (already documented, line 162-170)
   - `timeouts.tools.sequential_call` (already documented, line 768-774)
   - and document that the per-peer `a2a_agents.<peer>.timeout` is double-clipped by these when the call runs through the concurrent batch.

A short-term workaround is `HERMES_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S=3600` on the caller pod's env, but it caps the *whole batch*, not per-tool, so an uninterruptible long a2a_call still blocks every other tool in the same batch.

## Related

- #78007 — A2A: long tasks can never complete — client timeout (120s) dies before the server reply window (300s), raw-URL calls can't raise it
- #91167 — a2a_call: support indefinite (no-socket-timeout) peer calls
- #106972 — A2A: A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT does not affect the orphan-task sweep (hardcoded 300s) — late replies get silently discarded
- janpuc/home-ops#1372 — caller-side symptom report from the field

issues.body:
## Summary

On Windows 11, multi-profile gateway setup (one multiplex master serving several profiles), Kanban worker runs stopped receiving their prompt after the update from v0.22.2-era to **v0.22.5** (released 2026-10-23). The dispatcher spawns the worker, the worker process stays alive, `owner_admitted` and `worker_bound` events are written, but the prompt frame is **never written to the worker's stdin**. The worker idles in `read_frame` until `max_runtime_seconds` expires. 100% reproducible since the first Kanban use after the update.

## Timeline / evidence

- Last green Kanban worker run on this machine: **2026-10-10** (v0.22.2 era).
- Hermes updated to **v0.22.5** on 2026-10-23 (binary mtime + release timestamp match).
- First Kanban dispatch attempts after the update (2026-10-29 onward): every single run follows the identical pattern below. Several cards burned 4h timeouts each before the cause was understood.

## Observable pattern per run (default board, profile `allgemein`, gateway-routed)

1. Dispatcher claims task, spawns `hermes ... kanban worker` process, writes `claim_accepted`, `spawned`, `owner_admitted` (session_id present), `worker_bound` (pid present) into `task_events`.
2. Worker process is healthy but blocked: `py-spy dump` stack:
   `read_frame (kanban_worker_client.py:429) -> _dispatch_turn_worker (session_kanban.py:817) -> run (threading.py)`
3. **No LLM request ever leaves the worker**: zero `API call` lines for the worker session in `logs/agent.log`; proxy-side access log confirms zero requests from these sessions.
4. Run ends in `timed out` (or `crashed (pid gone)` when the timeout kill lands), `consecutive_failures` increments, after 3 strikes `gave_up`.
5. Manual `kanban_complete`/comments via tools work fine against the same task.

## What is NOT the cause (checked and measured)

- Model/LLM backend healthy (chat completions, streaming, embedding endpoint all verified green with curl while workers were stuck).
- Memory plugin (mem0) healthy and even patched for oversized-embed 400s; worker never gets far enough to touch memory.
- Session admission ledger clean (`session_admissions` 62/62 terminal after recovery; stale `started` rows from mid-run gateway restarts were a separate, secondary issue that also settles via restart).
- Same-profile interactive chat (Telegram + API server + `-z` oneshot) works concurrently on the same gateway, same profile, same minute. Only the Kanban worker prompt delivery is dead.

## Environment

- Windows 11, Hermes stable channel v0.22.5 (single install, `daemon` command not supported on this platform)
- Multiplexed gateway serving 10+ profiles; Kanban boards: default + several named boards
- Dispatcher runs inside the gateway process (`[dispatcher] tick complete`)

## Expected behavior

After `worker_bound`, the worker client receives a `prompt.request` frame on stdin and starts the agent turn (this is what happened on pre-v0.22.5 on this exact machine/config, last confirmed 2026-10-10).

## Actual behavior

Worker admitted and bound, then nothing: no `prompt.request` frame, worker idles at stdin until timeout.

## Additional data points

- Gateway restart with admission recovery (all admissions settled to terminal) does **not** fix delivery; next run shows the identical stall.
- Removing a slow MCP server (canva) from profile config did not change the pattern.
- `hermes -p <profile> -z "..."` (in-process oneshot) on the same profile succeeds seconds later, so the agent pipeline itself is fine.

Happy to provide anonymized `task_events` exports, py-spy dumps or gateway logs. Suspect something in the gateway->worker dispatch path changed between v0.22.2 and v0.22.5 (session_kanban dispatch / admission receipt handshake); bisecting releases on this machine is possible if that helps.

issues.body:
Body: _start_webhook_mode (plugins/platforms/telegram/adapter.py) calls updater.start_webhook() without cert/key, so the webhook server is plain HTTP — deployments must add a TLS reverse proxy, and since no certificate is uploaded, the endpoint needs a CA-valid cert (domain + Let's Encrypt).
>
 PTB's Updater.start_webhook already accepts cert/key: it serves TLS locally and uploads the certificate via set_webhook(certificate=...). Exposing two scoped secrets unlocks Telegram's documented self-signed-cert pattern for IP-based webhook URLs — no proxy, no domain, no renewal:
>
 
> webhook_cert = (_get_scoped_secret("TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_CERT") or "").strip() or None
> webhook_key = (_get_scoped_secret("TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_KEY") or "").strip() or None
> # pass cert=webhook_cert, key=webhook_key to start_webhook(...)
> ```
> ~6 lines, fully backward-compatible (None → current behavior). Our home deployment (public IP, no domain, port-forwarded) cut ~2M polling connections/month to ~0 with zero extra infrastructure using this pattern.

**维护须知（一条）**：每次 `hermes update` 后跑一下：

bash ~/scripts/repatch_tg_webhook_certkey.sh
```

issues.title: tests: home_io_guard fails on _payload_manifest() probing a non-existent ~/.hermes/manifest.json when the checkout lives inside ~/.hermes

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: tool/file
labels.description: File tools (read, write, patch, search)

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
## Summary

When a Hermes checkout lives **inside the guarded home** (the common
`~/.hermes/hermes-agent` layout), `_payload_manifest()` probes
`root.parent / "manifest.json"` as an ordinary first candidate. That path is
`~/.hermes/manifest.json`, which `tests/conftest.py::_capture_real_hermes_root()`
guards unconditionally. The guard fires on the **existence probe alone**, so
seven tests fail on a perfectly healthy install where the file does not exist.

Reporter environment: clawd (Debian 13, kernel 6.12.118), Hermes `main` @
`c84e8d7f81a8a12860dd802c24910c74115e36b6`, Python 3.14.9, 2026-11-25.

## Reproduction

```
$ cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent          # checkout inside the guarded home
$ scripts/run_tests.sh tests/pm/test_leases_outside_generations.py \
                       tests/pm/test_runtime.py \
                       tests/pm/test_startup_activation.py
=== Summary: 3 files, 27 tests passed, 6 failed, 1 skipped ===

FAILED test_leases_outside_generations.py::test_pm_runtime_launch_writes_only_leases_and_locks
FAILED test_runtime.py::test_one_store_through_symlinked_homes_keeps_one_pm_runtime
FAILED test_startup_activation.py::test_startup_uses_one_verdict  [×4]
```

All six fail identically:

```
pm/runtime.py:152:  env = runtime_environment()
pm/runtime.py:32:   env["HERMES_RUNTIME_DIR"] = native(store_root())
pm/paths.py:44:     return resolve(repo_root())
pm/environments.py:269: payload = _payload_manifest(root)
pm/environments.py:197: manifest = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig"))
tests/home_io_guard.py:160: AssertionError: TEST BUG: file I/O against the REAL hermes home:
                            /home/wahid/.hermes/manifest.json
```

## The file does not exist

```
$ ls /home/wahid/.hermes/manifest.json
ls: cannot access '/home/wahid/.hermes/manifest.json': No such file or directory
```

So nothing is being read; the failure is the **stat/open probe of a
non-existent path**. `_payload_manifest()` documents that this probe must be
harmless — its own docstring says a manifest some other tool left beside a
checkout "must read as *not a payload*, never as an error" — but the guard turns
the probe into an error.

## Why `HERMES_HOME` does not help

The natural workaround is an isolated home. It does not work, because the guard
adds the default root **unconditionally** (`tests/conftest.py`):

```python
default_root = (Path.home() / ".hermes").resolve()
roots.append(default_root)     # "hardcoded restatements hit it"
```

Verified with `HERMES_HOME` pointed at a fresh `mktemp -d`: identical 6 failures,
identical guarded path.

## The probe follows the checkout, not the home

The guard blames `root.parent / "manifest.json"` for whatever checkout root is
loaded, so the failure relocates with the checkout as long as that parent is
inside the guarded tree:

| checkout | guarded path blamed |
|---|---|
| `~/.hermes/hermes-agent` | `/home/wahid/.hermes/manifest.json` |
| `~/.hermes/cache/scratch/baseline-checkout` | `/home/wahid/.hermes/cache/scratch/manifest.json` |

Both fail identically. A checkout outside `~/.hermes` (e.g. `~/src/hermes-agent`)
should not hit this, but that is not the layout `hermes` installs itself into.

## Impact

`~/.hermes/hermes-agent` is the standard install location, so this trips on the
default configuration of a self-updating install. Seven pm tests are unpassable
on such a box without patching test infrastructure.

## Possible fixes

Any one of:

1. **Exempt existence probes.** In `HomeIOGuard.check`, allow `metadata=True`
   probes (stat/access) on a path whose file does not exist — reading nothing is
   not reading Hermes state. Only refuse when the path exists.
2. **Skip the sibling probe for guarded roots.** `_payload_manifest()` could
   treat an `OSError` from a guarded root as "not a payload" — but the guard is
   test-only, so production should not be taught about it.
3. **Exempt the sibling probe path.** Have the guard ignore
   `<repo_root>.parent / "manifest.json"` when the repo root is a source
   checkout (it carries `install-stamp.json` / `pyproject.toml`), since
   `_payload_manifest` is required to probe it.
4. **Document/test-only:** run the suite from a checkout outside `~/.hermes`.
   Acceptable as a workaround, but it silently moves the problem rather than
   fixing it.

Option 1 is the most principled: the guard's purpose is to stop tests *reading
or writing real Hermes state*. Probing for a file that does not exist touches no
state.

## Note

This is independent of the `members_stamp()` churn bug (#160196). That one makes
`pm install` fail outright on this box; with that fix applied the suite runs and
these 6/7 remain, so they are not downstream of it.

issues.body:
**Two independent defects in the Desktop-fleet message path**, measured on a live two-machine fleet (macOS console + Linux peer, both Hermes v0.22.2 `d923a5eb487a`), reproduced at BOTH ends.

**(A) `roster.json` attribution flap.** `~/.hermes/bot_relay/roster.json` is rewritten every ~20-60 s with the same agent rows but an alternating `connection_id`/`connection_label` — sometimes the owning remote connection, sometimes `local`/`"This device"`. The message layer resolves bare target names against this file, so `message_agent` is intermittent: the same target resolves in one window and lands on the local agent (`This device/@hermes`) in the next.

**(B) machine-root `bot_peers` gap.** The tool/roster layer reads `bot_peers` from the MACHINE-ROOT `config.yaml`, while `hermes peer list` reads the PROFILE-scoped one. A machine whose root has no `bot_peers` shows a healthy `hermes peer list` and an EMPTY tool-layer registry, so every bare-name cross-machine send falls to `This device`.

## (A) Measurements (sampling every 12 s; a single read is a coin flip)
MacAir: `16:18:53 | connection_id=['local'] | label=['This device']` -> `16:19:33 | ['delinux01'] | ['delinux01.local']` -> `16:19:53 | ['local'] | ['This device']`
Peer machine (60 s sampling): `local` -> `macair` -> `local`, same rows.
Rows are constant (`hermes/default`, `gozcu/gozcu`, `webmaster/webmaster` / `aikonsol`, `akillibidik`, `hermes/default`); only the ownership label oscillates. Each side's single read was correct at that instant, so the two records initially contradicted each other.
**Episodic, not constant:** a later 108 s sample was stable at one label — reproduce around connection-state events (Desktop pane open/close, remote reconnect).
Repro: read `~/.hermes/bot_relay/roster.json` every >=10 s; print `updated_at` + sorted `connection_id`s; assert >1 distinct set.

## (A) Writer chain (from source)
1. Desktop bots-relay plugin `apps/desktop/src/plugins/hermes-bots/relay.ts:486` -> `host.requestProfile(connection.route, 'bot_relay.roster.sync', { agents: others })` (`:412` pushes `{ agents: [] }` on disconnect).
2. Gateway RPC `tui_gateway/methods_bot_relay.py:54` (`@method("bot_relay.roster.sync")`) -> `:70` `write_remote_roster(_root(), params.get("agents"))`.
3. `tools/bot_relay.py:153 write_remote_roster()` -> `:160` `_atomic_write_json(...)` — writes incoming rows VERBATIM, no normalisation.

**Impact:** `tools/bot_mode_dm.py:248-253` — a bare target matches `_LOCAL_TARGET_RE`, resolves against the local roster, lands on `This device/@hermes` when the flap says `local`.

**Fix (either):** (1) Desktop: never emit a remote agent row attributed to the local connection. (2) Server: in `write_remote_roster()`, normalise/reject rows whose `connection_id` is the local connection while the agent is remote.

## (B) Root cause + evidence + fix
`tools/bot_mode_probe.py:_peers()` -> `_read_yaml_dict(root/'config.yaml','bot_peers')` reads the machine-root config; `hermes_cli/subcommands/peer.py:_load_peers()` -> `load_config()` reads the profile-scoped one. The code states it — `tools/bot_mode_dm.py:258-260`: "hermes peer resolves bot_peers via the profile-scoped load_config(), while the roster above reads the machine-root config ... a secondary-profile bot sees an empty registry".
Measured: root `bot_peers` absent -> `_peers(root)` `[]`; after adding `bot_peers: {macair: {url: http://127.0.0.1:18642}}` -> `['macair']`. Control on the console (root has 3 peers) -> `['aikonsol','akillibidik','delinux01']`.
**No gateway restart needed** — `_read_yaml_dict` re-reads the file per call (no config-loader import; `needle` is only a substring pre-check).
**Fix:** write peer entries into the machine-root `config.yaml` (what the code expects); the profile scope is for the CLI only.

**Addressing rule (measured):** the target grammar is `<peer>/<profile>`, not `<peer>/<handle>` — `macair/hermes` returns HTTP 404 while `macair/default` delivers (root profile is `default`; `hermes` is only its display handle; the route is `/p/default`).

## Pitfalls worth documenting
- Bare connection name (`macair`) matches `_LOCAL_TARGET_RE` and resolves against the local roster -> `This device/@hermes`, although the name "exists" in `connections.json`/the roster.
- Probing Hermes internals from a bare `python3` gives FALSE NEGATIVES: `_read_yaml_dict` does `import hermes_yaml` inside a `_swallow`, so `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ruamel'` is swallowed and `_peers()` returns `[]` for a config that DOES list peers. Use the runtime interpreter (`~/.hermes/tools/python-*/bin/python3`) with the uv-archive dep dir on `sys.path` (`~/.hermes/cache/uv/archive-v0/*/`), and control-measure on a machine whose answer is known.
- A `cp`-ed config backup can carry the source file's mtime, so the `.bak-<timestamp>` name and the mtime disagree — name = copy time, mtime = source's. Not an error, but say which you used.

labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/plugins
labels.description: Plugin system and bundled plugins

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: area/profiles
labels.description: Multi-profile isolation, HERMES_HOME scoping

issues.body:
**Summary.** With one multiplexed gateway serving several profiles, three A2A settings resolve against the
launch profile instead of the profile that serves the request.

1. **Reply window.** `plugins/platforms/a2a/adapter.py` reads `A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT` with plain
   `os.getenv(...)` (`_reply_timeout`). On the HTTP handler threads this is the launch profile's environment, so a
   served profile's own `.env` value is silently ignored. Observed: a served profile set
   `A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT=1500`, yet all of 442 tasks over 30 days were capped at exactly 300 s, the launch profile's
   value.
2. **Ping-pong cap.** `protocol.max_pingpong_turns()` (`A2A_MAX_PINGPONG_TURNS`) is read the same way, so the
   per-profile values do not apply either.
3. **Conversation log.** `protocol._conv_path()` builds `get_hermes_home() / "a2a_conversations" /
   f"{ctx}.jsonl"` without a profile scope. Server-side and client-side entries for the same context end up in
   one file under the launch home, with duplicate entries, and nothing is written under the served profiles.
   Anything that later relies on these logs, `a2a_history` or late-reply persistence for example, inherits the
   ambiguity.

**Expected.** Read these settings through the scoped secret and config lookup (`_get_scoped_secret` or
equivalent), as other per-profile secrets already are. Write conversation logs under the serving profile's home,
or key them so that server and client sides stay distinct.

**Workaround.** Set the values once in the launch profile's `.env`, which then apply process-wide.

**Environment.** Hermes Agent v0.23.4, `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true`.
